Redwood Trust Inc operates as a mortgage real estate investment trust focused on residential housing credit across four business segments. The company's Sequoia Mortgage Banking segment functions as a conduit acquiring residential consumer loans—primarily prime jumbo mortgages and adjustable-rate mortgages—from third-party originators for securitization through its proprietary SEMT securitization program, portfolio retention, or whole loan sales. The CoreVest Mortgage Banking segment originates residential investor loans including DSCR loans, bridge loans, and Residential Transition Loans (RTL products) for securitization or portfolio transfer. Redwood Investments holds retained securities sourced through these platforms as well as third-party real estate securities, while the Legacy Investments segment houses non-core assets in runoff. The company also manages mortgage servicing rights and home equity investments. All operations are U.S.-focused. In fiscal 2025, the company reported a net loss of $70 million, reflecting fair value losses on legacy unsecuritized bridge and term loan portfolios driven by increased delinquencies and credit stress.

Three pending litigation matters and a regulatory inquiry create near-term uncertainty. A loan seller has sued Redwood and others regarding pandemic-era loan purchase activities; separately, Redwood faces potential indirect exposure through Student Loan ABS securitization entity liability based on third-party servicer conduct. Early 2026 class action lawsuits were filed against two third-party HEI originators (not Redwood directly) alleging unlicensed mortgage lending and consumer protection violations, though these could impact Redwood's HEI investment portfolio. The Washington State Department of Financial Institutions issued a request for information in 2026 regarding Redwood's HEI originations and ownership involving Washington State residents. Additionally, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau filed an amicus brief in 2025 expressing views that HEI constitutes a residential mortgage loan and credit subject to TILA, signaling continued regulatory scrutiny of this product category.

Redwood operates in a highly competitive landscape dominated by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which the company acknowledges limits private-sector opportunities. The company faces competition from commercial banks, other mortgage REITs, regional banks, broker-dealers, and specialty finance firms. Redwood positions itself on control over underwriting and collateral review for sourced investments, best-in-class securitization infrastructure, and access to underserved segments. However, the company acknowledges stated disadvantages: competitors with greater resources and lower funding costs, potential inability to compete against higher-risk-tolerance competitors, and structural constraints on available opportunities due to GSE dominance in mortgage finance.

During 2025, Redwood established the Legacy Investments segment to accelerate wind-down of non-core assets and in Q3 sold $484 million in fair value of legacy unsecuritized bridge loans and REO assets to Legacy Trust. The company launched the Aspire mortgage loan conduit in Q1 2025 to serve expanded-credit borrowers. Forward initiatives include CoreVest growth in RTL and DSCR small-balance products, scaling of Sequoia securitization infrastructure, and joint venture partnerships for capital efficiency. An $89 million goodwill impairment was recorded in 2020 related to the 5 Arches and CoreVest acquisitions.

### NGVT
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1653477/000165347726000014/ngvt-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $307M impairment disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

Ingevity Corp operates three distinct business segments serving industrial and transportation end markets. Revenue declined 2.7% to $1.18 billion in the most recent fiscal year, with gross margin holding at 39.5%. The Performance Materials segment engineers activated carbon products derived from hardwood for automotive emissions control in internal combustion engines and hybrid vehicles, as well as for food, water, and chemical filtration. Performance Chemicals comprises pavement technologies—producing asphalt additives and preservation products—and road markings, which manufactures thermoplastic and waterborne paint technologies. Advanced Polymer Technologies manufactures caprolactone-based specialty polymers for coatings, resins, elastomers, adhesives, bioplastics, and medical applications. The company operates primarily in North America, Asia Pacific, and China, with secondary presence in Europe, South Korea, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Ingevity positions itself on decades of track record in emissions standards compliance, proprietary manufacturing know-how, strong intellectual property protection, and deep customer relationships in road-building and automotive domains.

The company disclosed a $307 million impairment charge across two reporting units in fiscal 2025, driven by tariff impacts, macroeconomic uncertainty, and advanced divestiture diligence. Goodwill impairment for Advanced Polymer Technologies totaled $183.8 million; long-lived asset impairment for the Performance Chemicals road markings group reached $109.3 million. Separately, Ingevity faces material litigation exposure: the Federal Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the company on February 11, 2026, in a BASF patent infringement case, upholding a jury verdict of $28.3 million in damages that was trebled to $85.0 million. The company expects to make payment in Q2 2026 plus post-judgment interest, with total exposure now estimated at $95.4 million. These charges contributed to net loss of $167.1 million in the fiscal year. Additionally, a cooperation agreement with Vision One Fund requires the board to appoint a new member within one day of the 2025 annual meeting.

Customer concentration presents material risk across segments. In Performance Materials—the largest by revenue concentration—the ten largest customers represent approximately 90 percent of sales. Within Performance Chemicals, the top ten customers account for 32 percent of segment revenue, though concentration is higher in sub-segments: pavement technologies at 38 percent and road markings at 59 percent. Advanced Polymer Technologies' top ten customers represent 44 percent of sales. On the supply side, hydrogen peroxide is sourced from a single supplier, Solvay Interox Limited, while hardwood sawdust and phosphoric acid come through multiple vendors. Manufacturing footprint includes exposure to China for Performance Materials and the United Kingdom for Advanced Polymer Technologies. The company operates with stated disadvantages including limited multi-site manufacturing capability for certain products and dependency on third parties for critical operating services at some plants. Competitive pressures include accelerated EV adoption reducing internal combustion engine demand, particularly in Europe, and alternative-fueled vehicle adoption broadly constraining growth.

Ingevity is executing a strategic portfolio review that simplifies the company to two core segments. The company completed the sale of its Industrial Specialties product line to Mainstream Pine Products, LLC, effective January 1, 2026, which is expected to eliminate $15 million in stranded costs during 2026. Advanced Polymer Technologies exploration for sale is targeted by end of 2026, as is divestiture of the Performance Chemicals road markings business. Capital expenditure is planned at $50 million, with a range of $40 million to $60 million. Guidance for the current period projects revenue of $1.15 billion, with a range of $1.1 billion to $1.2 billion, and EPS of $5.0.

### BTU

_Triggers: 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: EPA, Department of Justice._

Peabody Energy Corp operates as a diversified coal producer with four principal segments: Seaborne Thermal (surface mining of low-sulfur thermal coal in New South Wales), Seaborne Metallurgical (underground and surface mining in Queensland, New South Wales, and Alabama), Powder River Basin (surface mining in Wyoming), and Other U.S. Thermal (mixed extraction across Illinois, Indiana, New Mexico, and Colorado). The company maintains 16 active mining operations across the United States and Australia. Revenue declined 8.9% to $3.86 billion in the most recent fiscal period from $4.24 billion in the prior year, with net income swinging to a loss of $52.9 million. Peabody positions itself as a leading producer of both metallurgical and thermal coal, emphasizing its modern loading facilities, secured rail and port transport contracts, and a backlog of approximately 238 million tons with terms extending up to seven years.

The company faces material litigation originating from a terminated asset purchase with Anglo American subsidiaries. Anglo initiated International Chamber of Commerce arbitration proceedings contesting Peabody's assertion that a Moranbah North mine ignition event on March 31, 2025 constituted a Material Adverse Change triggering termination rights under metallurgical coal asset purchase agreements. Anglo seeks declarations negating the Material Adverse Change claim and damages in unspecified amount. Concurrently, the regulatory landscape has shifted substantially in Peabody's favor. The EPA announced on March 12, 2025 that it will reconsider multiple prior actions including GHG emissions regulations, air quality standards, mercury standards, and coal combustion residuals disposal rules. On June 17, 2025, the EPA proposed repeal of all GHG emissions standards for new and existing fossil fuel-fired power plants. The EPA finalized rescission of its 2009 endangerment finding regarding greenhouse gas regulation under the Clean Air Act on February 12, 2026. The Bureau of Land Management announced on September 29, 2025 that it is making up to 13.1 million acres of federal coal available for lease with lowered royalty rates and streamlined approvals. The Department of Justice filed complaints against Michigan, Hawaii, New York, and Vermont regarding climate superfund laws and fossil fuel company liability. Offsetting these regulatory developments, Queensland appointed its first Mining and Resources Coroner in early 2025 with authority to investigate fatalities and issue mandatory safety recommendations.

Peabody's structural position reflects meaningful headwinds embedded in coal demand fundamentals. The company discloses that U.S. coal power capacity has declined 46% since 2010, with significant coal plant retirements reducing thermal coal demand. Metallurgical coal demand faces pressure from electric arc furnace adoption in steel manufacturing. The company's five largest customers represent 25% of coal supply agreement revenue, with the largest customer contributing approximately 8% of total revenue. Heavy reliance on long-term supply agreements containing price reopener provisions introduces margin volatility. Substantial take-or-pay arrangements convert variable costs to fixed costs, constraining flexibility during demand downturns. The company faces competition from producers of alternative energy sources (natural gas, oil, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar, biomass) and from numerous named competitors spanning U.S. regional producers, international seaborne exporters, and vertically integrated mining companies. Exposure to foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations affects Australian operations.

Peabody has planned capital expenditures of $340 million. Key operational initiatives include commencement of full-scale longwall production at Centurion Mine in February 2026 and development of a rare earth element and critical mineral recovery pilot plant funded by the Wyoming Energy Authority, with processing development underway for Powder River Basin rare earth elements and critical minerals. The company experienced operational disruptions during the period: Wambo Underground Mine ceased production in September 2025 following the Moranbah North ignition event in March 2025 that led to mine closure; lock outages along the Black Warrior River in Alabama during 2024 neg

### AMR
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1704715/000170471526000010/amr-20251231.htm)_

Alpha Metallurgical Resources operates a single reportable segment focused on metallurgical and thermal coal mining and sales. The company generated $2.13 billion in revenue during the filing period, representing a 28% decline from $2.96 billion in the prior year. AMR mines primarily in Virginia and West Virginia, with significant export exposure to Asia and secondary markets in Europe and the domestic United States. Beyond coal extraction, the company derives revenue from equipment sales, royalties, natural gas, terminal and processing fees, and coal analysis services. The company positions itself on high-quality reserves in the CAPP coal basin, significant port capacity at its DTA terminal, operational flexibility across multiple mines, established customer relationships, and coal blending capabilities. Safety performance runs 38% better than industry average. However, the company faces headwinds from concentrated production across a small number of material mines, dependence on a single rail carrier for most operations, and reliance on third-party trucking. Customer concentration is acute: the top 10 customers represent 77% of revenues. The company competes against Appalachian, Illinois basin, and western coal producers, as well as Australian and Canadian exporters, alongside alternative energy sources including natural gas, nuclear, renewables, and electric arc furnace steelmaking.

The revenue decline reflects operational disruptions and market softness that cascaded through 2024 and into 2025. Rolling Thunder mine experienced water inundation in November 2025 requiring recovery costs and idling. Checkmate Powellton was temporarily idled in November 2024 due to softening met coal markets and high startup costs. Long Branch surface mine idled in Q1 2025 due to continued weakness in met coal pricing. Jerry Fork and Black Eagle mines saw production reductions tied to weak global steel demand and U.S. High-Vol. product pricing pressure. Beyond operational challenges, AMR faces a multi-front regulatory and litigation environment. In February 2025, the company filed a federal complaint challenging New York's Climate Change Superfund Act adopted in December 2024, which imposes significant ongoing cash charges on fossil fuel producers; the DOJ and EPA filed a similar complaint in May 2025. MSHA issued a final rule in April 2024 lowering the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica to 50 μg/m³, with a compliance deadline of April 14, 2025, though a temporary administrative stay was granted by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on April 4, 2025. The DOL published a final rule in January 2025 revising black lung self-insurance collateral requirements to 100% minimum, with the company estimating an $80–100 million additional collateral requirement. The EPA finalized rules in late 2024 addressing coal combustion residuals management and revised the PM2.5 primary annual standard downward to 9.0 μg/m³ in February 2024, alongside more stringent MATS emission standards for power generators.

The company's structural position is shaped by its dependence on metallurgical coal exports and exposure to volatile global steel demand. With top 10 customers at 77% of revenues and production concentrated in a small number of material mines, AMR carries meaningful customer and operational concentration risk. Reliance on a single rail carrier for most operations and third-party trucking services creates supply chain vulnerability. Skilled labor shortage in the mining industry compounds execution risk. Environmental and regulatory compliance costs are stringent; the company uses multiple non-GAAP measures including Adjusted EBITDA, non-GAAP coal margins, and per-ton metrics, suggesting earnings volatility and the need for normalized comparisons. Net income was negative $61.7 million during the filing period.

Capital expenditure is planned at $158 million, with a range of $148–168 million. Key initiatives include Kingston Wildcat underground mine production commencing Q1 2026, DTA infrastructure upgrades averaging $21 million annually over five years, Section 45X metallurgical coal tax credit eligibility for 2026–2029, and

### RXO
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1929561/000192956126000013/rxo-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; acquisition $1.0B disclosed._

RXO, Inc. operates as a brokered transportation platform serving North America with a comprehensive service portfolio spanning truck brokerage, managed transportation, last mile services, freight forwarding, ocean and air transportation, customs brokerage, and ground and air express. The company generated $5.74 billion in revenue in fiscal 2025, representing 26.2% growth from $4.55 billion in the prior year. However, this expansion masks operational challenges: gross margin stood at 19.7%, while the company posted a negative operating margin of -1.4% and a net loss of $100 million. RXO positions itself as one of the largest full truckload freight brokers in North America and the largest provider of outsourced last mile transportation for heavy goods in the U.S., competing against established players including C.H. Robinson, J.B. Hunt, Landstar System, Echo Global Logistics, Expeditors, and technology-driven entrants like Uber Freight and Flexport.

RXO faces two pending litigation exposures that warrant investor attention. The company is defending class action and collective action lawsuits claiming that third-party carriers or their delivery workers should be classified as employees rather than independent contractors, with plaintiffs seeking unpaid wages, overtime, and reimbursed expenses. Separately, RXO is defending negligent selection claims from private litigants in highway accident cases alleging the broker was negligent in selecting unsafe carriers. Additionally, the company took a $12 million goodwill impairment charge on its ground and air express reporting unit in fiscal 2025 due to lower than anticipated operating results and changing market fundamentals. These legal and operational headwinds emerged as RXO integrated its $1.048 billion acquisition by United Parcel Service of America, Inc., completed in 2024.

Customer concentration presents a structural risk. The top 20 customers represent approximately 37% of 2025 revenue, with the top 5 accounting for 23% and the largest single customer representing $653 million or 11.4% of total revenue. RXO's competitive positioning rests on proprietary digital brokerage technology with stated first-mover advantage, access to extensive carrier relationships, machine learning-driven pricing algorithms, and an asset-light model. However, the company discloses material vulnerabilities: dependence on third-party carriers over which it has limited control, vulnerability to economic recessions and seasonal freight demand fluctuations, exposure to volatile fuel prices, and risk of customer disintermediation as shippers develop internal logistics capabilities. The potential reclassification of independent contractors as employees—already surfacing in pending litigation—represents a structural cost risk to the business model.

RXO's near-term focus centers on integrating and optimizing the Coyote acquisition, enhancing its RXO Connect digital platform, expanding managed transportation control tower capabilities, growing last mile services within 125-mile networks, and investing in artificial intelligence and machine learning infrastructure. The company has not provided revenue or earnings guidance for upcoming periods.

### AMN
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1142750/000162828026009918/amn-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $123M impairment disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

AMN Healthcare Services operates as a comprehensive healthcare staffing and workforce solutions provider across three primary segments. Nurse and Allied Solutions supplies temporary and permanent staffing for nursing and allied health professionals to hospitals and healthcare facilities, encompassing travel nurse placement, crisis staffing, labor disruption coverage, and revenue cycle solutions including medical coding and clinical documentation. Physician and Leadership Solutions provides locum tenens staffing for physicians and advanced practice professionals, interim executive and clinical leadership placement, and permanent physician placement services. Technology and Workforce Solutions delivers language interpretation services, vendor management systems and managed services programs, recruitment process outsourcing, and workforce optimization consulting. The company operates primarily in the United States and recruits internationally for nurse staffing. Revenue declined 8.5% to $2.73 billion in fiscal 2025 from $2.98 billion in the prior year, with gross margin at 28.3% and operating margin negative at negative 2.0%, yielding a net loss of $95.7 million.

The company recorded $127.8 million in aggregate impairment charges in fiscal 2025, consisting of a $109.5 million goodwill impairment in the Physician and Leadership Solutions segment and an $18.3 million impairment on customer relationship intangibles in the Revenue Cycle Solutions business. These charges follow substantial impairments in fiscal 2024, when the company recorded $222.5 million in combined goodwill impairments across Nurse and Allied Solutions ($123.3 million) and Physician and Leadership Solutions ($99.2 million). The company also completed a $65.3 million asset sale in fiscal 2025. Additionally, AMN Healthcare faces a pending class and representative action lawsuit involving wage and hour claims under California and Federal law, with financial exposure not yet quantified.

AMN Healthcare operates with concentrated customer exposure. Kaiser Foundation Hospitals and affiliates represented 22% of consolidated revenue in fiscal 2025 and 32% of Nurse and Allied Solutions segment revenue, creating material dependency on a single customer. The company competes against numerous national, regional, and local staffing providers including Aya Healthcare, CHG Healthcare Services, Cross Country Healthcare, Jackson Healthcare, and others, alongside hospital systems' internal recruitment operations. The company positions itself on a comprehensive solution suite, national scale, and established infrastructure including Joint Commission certification, though it faces headwinds from intense competitive pressure for qualified clinical talent, pricing pressure from consolidated healthcare buyers, and reliance on visa availability for international nurse recruitment. Recent technology investments include the WorkWise platform launched in 2024, expanded ShiftWise Flex VMS capabilities with automation, AMN Passport extension to locum tenens providers, and AI-enabled automation in recruiting and credentialing.

The company provided no revenue or earnings guidance for upcoming periods. Capital expenditure plans were not disclosed. Disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting were assessed as effective, and no material weaknesses, restatements, or going concern issues were identified. KPMG LLP serves as the auditor.

### PII
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/931015/000162828026008033/pii-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $330M impairment disclosed; 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

Polaris Inc. operates three core business segments across recreational and utility vehicles, with revenue flat at $7.2 billion in the latest fiscal year. The Off Road segment manufactures ATVs, side-by-side vehicles, snowmobiles, and commercial/defense vehicles. The On Road segment produces motorcycles, moto-roadsters, and light duty vehicles. The Marine segment builds pontoon and deck boats under the Bennington, Godfrey, and Hurricane brands. The company maintains a primary presence in the United States, Canada, Western Europe, and Mexico, with secondary operations in Australia. Polaris positions itself as the North American market share leader in off-road vehicles and pontoon boats, and holds the number two position in North American snowmobiles, supported by an extensive network of approximately 600 global dealers and a full line of 90 ORV models across multiple price points.

The filing reflects significant asset write-downs totaling $330 million tied to the Indian Motorcycle business, which is being held for sale. Beyond the divestiture, goodwill impairments of $52.6 million were recorded for the On Road segment due to continued financial decline and deteriorating industry conditions, and separate indefinite-lived intangible asset charges of $53.9 million affected the Off Road segment related to changes in planned asset usage. The company faces two pending class action lawsuits—Guzman/Albright and Berlanga—consolidated in federal court regarding rollover protection structure certifications on off-road vehicles. Both cases were certified for money damages claims under California law, though trial dates were vacated in February 2025, leaving the ultimate financial exposure unquantified.

The business operates with structural vulnerabilities. Gross margin of 19.1 percent compresses further when considering an operating margin of negative 4.9 percent, resulting in a net loss of $465.5 million. The company sources components from tariff-subject countries for facilities in the United States and Mexico, exposing it to trade policy shifts. Stated disadvantages include competition from more diversified manufacturers with superior production footprints, exposure to commodity and raw material volatility, single-source component risks, and reliance on dealer and distributor networks beyond direct control. The company competes against both North American and Asian off-road manufacturers, Japanese snowmobile competitors, and established boat builders, with some competitors investing more heavily in product development and marketing.

The Indian Motorcycle business majority interest sale is scheduled to complete in Q1 2026. Near-term product initiatives include redesigned RZR and RANGER models, new Bennington and Godfrey boat variants, and the Ranger 500 mid-size utility vehicle. No revenue or earnings guidance has been provided.

### ROG

_Triggers: 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; CEO changed during fiscal year._

Rogers Corp manufactures engineered materials and components across three operating segments. Advanced Electronics Solutions designs and produces circuit materials, ceramic substrates, busbars, and cooling solutions for electric vehicles, automotive advanced driver assistance systems, aerospace and defense, renewable energy, wireless infrastructure, and industrial applications. Elastomeric Material Solutions develops polyurethane and silicone materials for cushioning, gasketing, sealing, and vibration management, along with specialized silicones for thermal applications and fluoropolymer materials. A smaller Other segment covers elastomer components and floats for industrial and fuel-tank sensing applications. The company operates across North America, Europe, and Asia, with secondary manufacturing and operations in China, Germany, England, Belgium, South Korea, and Hungary. Rogers positions itself on differentiated, high-performance materials, a history of innovation, technical expertise, product quality, a broad product line, and design engineering services. Revenue declined 2.3% to $810.8 million in fiscal 2025, while gross margin compressed to 31.7% and the company reported an operating margin of -5.6% with a net loss of $61.7 million.

The filing discloses a pending asbestos-related product liability matter stemming from operations before the 1990s, with estimated liabilities of $57.4 million through 2064 and anticipated insurance recoveries of $52.8 million. A goodwill impairment of $67.3 million was recorded on the curamik® reporting unit within the Advanced Electronics Solutions segment, driven by reduced demand forecasts reflecting changing market competition and supply dynamics. Additional impairment charges of $1.9 million related to a Mexico facility lease and $7.9 million tied to an ERP system still in development further pressured profitability. The company also terminated a joint venture with INOAC during 2024. A CEO transition occurred during the fiscal year. These events—particularly the substantial goodwill write-down and operating loss—signal deteriorating conditions in core business segments and execution challenges around system modernization and facility optimization.

Rogers faces material structural headwinds. The company relies on sole or limited-source suppliers for certain raw materials, while supply chain exposure concentrates in China and South Korea. No single customer exceeds 10% of sales, providing some diversification, but the company competes against manufacturers with greater financial resources, faces intense global pricing pressure, and operates in markets subject to macroeconomic volatility, inflation, foreign currency fluctuations, and trade tariffs. Stated competitive disadvantages also include dependence on customer adoption of new technologies and challenges protecting proprietary technology internationally. The company is executing several restructuring initiatives: wind-down of AES manufacturing at its Evergem, Belgium facility, consolidation of curamik® production at Eschenbach, Germany, exit from its Burlington, Massachusetts Innovation Center, sale of the Price Road facility, global workforce reduction, and ongoing curamik® reporting unit optimization.

Rogers plans capital expenditures in the range of $30 million to $40 million, with a midpoint of $35 million. Key forward initiatives include completion of the manufacturing footprint consolidation in Belgium and Germany, continued curamik® restructuring, global workforce reduction and executive transition execution, Innovation Centers focused on new material solutions development, and ERP system implementation and development. The company provided no revenue or earnings guidance for upcoming periods.

### CC

Chemours Co is a diversified chemical manufacturer operating across three primary segments: Thermal & Specialized Solutions, which supplies refrigerants, thermal management solutions, propellants, blowing agents, and specialty solvents; Titanium Technologies, which produces titanium dioxide pigment for whiteness and opacity applications; and Advanced Performance Materials, which develops high-performance polymers and advanced materials with properties including low friction, extreme temperature resistance, and chemical resistance. The company operates globally in approximately 110 countries with primary exposure to the United States and Europe, and secondary presence in Asia Pacific and Latin America. Revenue was essentially flat at $5.8 billion in 2025 compared to $5.8 billion in 2024, though the company reported a net loss of $386 million with an operating margin of negative 16.6% and gross margin of 15.5%, reflecting significant operational headwinds. Chemours positions itself on leadership in fluorine chemistry and materials science, proprietary chloride technology for titanium dioxide production, deep customer relationships spanning decades, and ability to operate complex manufacturing sites safely.

Litigation and regulatory actions create substantial near-term financial burdens and operational constraints. The company faces disclosed litigation exposure exceeding $943 million related to PFAS and PFOA contamination claims, with a settled New Jersey consent order requiring $875 million in annual payments over 25 years. Additional settled claims include $13.5 million from the Hoosick Falls class action and $10 million remaining from an Ohio settlement expected in the first half of 2026. Asbestos-related indemnification obligations total $96 million. The EPA has designated PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances under CERCLA as of April 2024 and established a final national drinking water regulation for six PFAS compounds with a five-year compliance deadline. The European Commission imposed a 200% quota reduction penalty on the Dordrecht Works facility for F-Gas regulation violations applicable in 2026, and the Dutch ILT agency collected €1 million in penalties in June 2025. An EU-wide PFAS restriction proposal under REACH affecting more than 4,000 substances including fluoropolymers and F-gases is estimated to enter force by 2027. The company received multiple EPA Administrative Orders on Consent regarding monitoring and remediation at the Washington Works facility.

Titanium Technologies carries concentrated customer exposure, with one customer representing over 20% of segment sales and the top 10 customers accounting for more than 44% of segment revenue, creating dependency risk distinct from other segments where no single customer exceeds 10% of sales. The company disclosed a $56 million goodwill impairment in Advanced Performance Materials in 2024 driven by lower hydrogen market demand projections and competitive headwinds, followed by $30 million in asset charges in 2025 including accelerated depreciation and inventory write-offs. Recent facility disruptions include shutdown of the Kuan Yin, Taiwan TiO2 facility with planned land sale expected mid-2026 generating approximately $360 million in proceeds intended for debt reduction, critical equipment damage at Washington Works following an August 2025 power outage with unscheduled downtime extending into 2026, and temporary idling of a Florida mineral sands mine in January 2026. Named competitors include Arkema S.A., Daikin Industries, Tronox Holdings, and expanding Chinese producers developing similar chloride production technology.

Planned capital expenditures total $250 million to $300 million for 2026. The company is executing its Pathway to Thrive corporate strategy, advancing the Titanium Technologies Transformation Plan for cost optimization, and expanding Opteon refrigerant capacity for data center cooling applications, with the Corpus Christi Opteon YF expansion approximately 40% complete as of Q4 2024. Michael Foley was welcomed as the new Titanium Technologies business president in February 2026. No revenue or earnings guidance has been provided.

Cohen & Steers is a global investment manager specializing in real assets and alternative income strategies. Revenue grew 7.5% to $556.1 million in the most recent fiscal year, with operating margin holding at 32%. The firm manages assets across open-end funds, closed-end funds, ETFs, and institutional accounts, with offerings spanning listed and private real estate, preferred securities, infrastructure, resource equities, commodities, and multi-strategy solutions. Its primary market is the United States, with secondary operations in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore. Cohen & Steers positions itself as a specialist manager with established track records, an integrated global investment team, and diversified distribution through wealth and institutional channels.

The company changed its CFO during the fiscal year, which represents a shift in senior financial leadership. Net income reached $153.2 million. Beyond this staffing change, the filing discloses no material litigation, regulatory actions, impairments, or other significant catalysts.

The firm's competitive position is shaped by meaningful structural constraints. Real estate securities strategies represent 63.8% of assets under management, creating heavy concentration in a single asset class. Cohen & Steers competes directly against passive strategies and index funds while facing fee compression from lower-cost rivals. The company is also dependent on third-party intermediaries for distribution and faces escalating regulatory compliance complexity across its global footprint. World Acceptance Corp operates a single Consumer Finance segment offering small and medium-term installment loans alongside credit insurance products and ancillary services. The company generated revenue of $564.8 million in the latest period, essentially flat compared to $573.2 million in the prior year, with an operating margin of 27.4% and net income of $89.7 million. The business spans 16 states, with Georgia, Illinois, and Texas as primary markets and the remainder as secondary. World Acceptance positions itself on a relatively large scale within small-loan consumer finance, emphasizing rapid branch-level loan approval, established credit scoring capabilities, and strong local community reputation. The company competes against banks, credit unions, online lenders, payday lenders, and other consumer finance firms.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau issued a public designation order establishing supervisory authority over World Acceptance in 2022 under 12 USC 5514(a)(1)(C). The CFPB withdrew this supervisory order on May 12, 2025, signaling a change in regulatory priorities affecting the company. This action occurred as World Acceptance undertook branch rationalization during fiscal 2025: the company acquired 3 new branches and spent $18.8 million on asset purchases from competitors and branch owners, but simultaneously merged or closed 27 branches, resulting in a net reduction of 24 branches. This consolidation reflects management's effort to concentrate operations in locations generating sufficient returns.

World Acceptance faces structural headwinds that define its competitive positioning. The company explicitly discloses higher delinquency and charge-off rates than traditional lenders, operates in a customer segment with limited access to traditional credit sources, and faces potential risk from federal usury caps that could eliminate its business model. Geographic concentration in 16 states creates regional risk exposure. Negative media characterization as predatory lending and competition from online lenders targeting the same customer segment add reputational and competitive pressure. The company is subject to extensive federal and state regulation and licensing requirements, with increasing regulatory scrutiny and associated compliance costs.

World Acceptance is pursuing multiple strategic initiatives including tax preparation program expansion across all branches, continued branch acquisition and new market entry, accelerated technology transformation for workforce management, and enhanced digital and online lending platform development. The company has also established a credit insurance reinsurance structure through a captive subsidiary. The company has not provided revenue or earnings guidance for future periods.

Verra Mobility Corp operates across three distinct segments serving the mobility and enforcement sectors. Commercial Services provides toll and violations management and title and registration solutions to rental car companies, fleet operators, and fleet management companies primarily across North America and Europe. Government Solutions delivers photo enforcement automated safety systems—including speed, red-light, school bus, and city bus lane enforcement—to states, municipalities, counties, school districts, and law enforcement agencies mainly in the United States, Canada, and Australia. Parking Solutions offers end-to-end parking management including software, transaction processing, hardware, and back-office systems to universities, municipalities, healthcare facilities, and commercial operators in the United States and Canada. Revenue grew 11.4% to $979.1 million, with gross margin of 92.3% and operating margin of 24.4%.

Verra Mobility settled a material class action lawsuit in the Brantley v. City of Gretna case challenging the legality of a safety camera program. The class was certified on March 30, 2021, with preliminary settlement approval granted in April 2025 and final approval on September 18, 2025. The company also recorded a $97.1 million goodwill impairment in the Parking Solutions segment in 2024 and a $9.4 million impairment of installation and service parts, property and equipment, and customer relationship intangible assets in 2025 related to an exit from Ontario, Canada. That exit followed the enactment of a ban on automated speed enforcement cameras in the province in November 2025.

The company's competitive position rests on long-standing relationships with the three largest rental car companies in the United States and more than 50 tolling authorities, alongside proprietary technologies for photo enforcement and parking management. However, customer concentration poses a structural risk, with NYCDOT representing 17.9% of total revenues. The company faces exposure to competitors with greater resources, potential competition from customers developing internal solutions, and the longer-term threat that advances in autonomous vehicles could reduce traffic violations. Political and regulatory risk is material: the company discloses risks of decreased acceptance of automated photo enforcement and potential governmental restrictions on enforcement and tolling.

Key forward catalysts include a five-year automated enforcement contract with NYCDOT valued at $998 million effective January 1, 2026, alongside expansion of city bus lane and school bus stop arm enforcement programs. The company is also investing in SaaS product offerings and professional services in Parking Solutions and growing European tolling and violations processing operations. In October 2025, the company refinanced debt, reducing the interest rate by 25 basis points.

### CSR
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/798359/000079835926000014/csr-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: regulatory action: Federal Trade Commission, U.S. Justice Department and State Attorneys General._

Centerspace owns, manages, and redevelops apartment communities across the Minneapolis/St. Paul, Denver, Boulder/Fort Collins, and Salt Lake City metropolitan areas. The company generated $273.7 million in revenue in its most recent fiscal year, a 4.9% increase from $261.0 million in the prior year, with an operating margin of 23.6%. Beyond apartment home rentals, the company derives additional revenue from commercial space leasing within its properties. Centerspace positions itself on focus in large, stable markets with growing economic conditions, operational enhancements to resident experience, and disciplined capital allocation targeting consistent earnings growth. It competes against other apartment communities, condominiums, single-family homes, short-term rentals, REITs, private partnerships, pension funds, and institutional real estate investors.

Recent regulatory developments in the broader multifamily sector create potential headwinds for the industry. In 2025, the U.S. Justice Department and several state Attorneys General filed complaints against six of the nation's largest landlords alleging antitrust violations related to algorithmic pricing schemes. Separately, the Federal Trade Commission filed a lawsuit against the nation's largest landlord for deceiving consumers by charging mandatory fees in addition to monthly rent. While Centerspace was not a party to these actions, the enforcement activity signals regulatory scrutiny of pricing and fee practices in the multifamily sector and introduces inquiry risk for other operators. During 2025, the company also recorded a $37.7 million impairment related to real estate investments—six apartment communities were written down to estimated fair value as they were held for sale and subsequently sold, and one community was written down based on independent appraisal.

Centerspace's portfolio concentration presents structural constraints. The company is heavily dependent on a single asset class—multifamily apartments—and operates exclusively in the Midwest and Mountain West regions. This geographic and product concentration limits diversification. The business is inherently exposed to resident rental payment performance and occupancy rate volatility. Short-term lease structures create vulnerability to market rent declines, and tight labor markets are driving higher compensation costs that may outpace rent growth. Real estate assets are relatively illiquid, constraining the company's ability to quickly dispose of properties if strategic repositioning becomes necessary.

During 2025, Centerspace completed two acquisitions—Railway Flats for $132.2 million and Sugarmont for $149.0 million—while divesting properties for $215.5 million in aggregate proceeds. The company is pursuing operational enhancements, redevelopment initiatives, technology leveraging for scaling, and selective acquisitions in its core markets. No specific revenue or earnings guidance was disclosed for forward periods, nor were capital expenditure plans quantified.

### WAY
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1990354/000199035426000011/way-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: acquisition $1.3B disclosed._

Waystar Holding Corp. provides AI-powered cloud-based software that streamlines healthcare payments across the full patient journey—from financial clearance and pre-encounter work through mid-encounter and post-encounter claims management, denials recovery, and analytics. Revenue grew 16.5% to $1.1 billion in 2025 from $944 million in 2024, with gross margin of 68.3% and operating margin of 22.7%. The company operates as a single segment focused on the U.S. market, positioning itself as a comprehensive end-to-end solution built on modern cloud architecture with proprietary AI capabilities and deep payer connectivity accumulated over two decades. Waystar emphasizes its 112% Net Revenue Retention Rate and 85% average win rate in competitive selections as evidence of client stickiness and competitive strength. Product capabilities span financial clearance, patient financial care, claims and payer payment management, denials prevention and recovery, clinical integrity and revenue capture, and analytics and reporting.

In 2025, Waystar completed the acquisition of Iodine for $1.26 billion. The company is integrating Iodine's AI-powered clinical intelligence capabilities into its platform and developing an autonomous revenue cycle initiative leveraging agentic AI as a forward strategic priority. This acquisition represents a material capital deployment and signals Waystar's intent to deepen its AI moat and expand its product scope beyond traditional payment workflows into clinical decision support.

Waystar faces structural headwinds typical of its market position. Top 10 clients account for only 10.8% of revenue, indicating reasonable customer diversification, though the company remains exposed to pricing pressures from consolidating healthcare providers and competition from well-resourced technology companies entering the space. Named competitive threats include large EHR and practice management system providers offering overlapping solutions, point solution vendors, revenue cycle specialists, and large technology firms with greater resources. The company acknowledges variable sales cycles of weeks to 18 months, implementation timing dependent on client resources, and reliance on third-party data providers and technology vendors. Regulatory and reimbursement changes in healthcare create ongoing exposure.

Waystar is pursuing client expansion through cross-sell and up-sell within existing relationships and deepening partnerships with EHR and PM providers. The company does not provide forward revenue or earnings guidance. Capital allocation beyond the Iodine acquisition is not detailed in the filing.

### HTO
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/766829/000162828026012438/hto-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

H2O America operates regulated water utility systems across California, Connecticut, Maine, and Texas through subsidiary companies including SJWC, CWC, TWC, and MWC. The company provides water and wastewater services alongside ancillary offerings such as Linebacker protection plans and real estate property management. Revenue grew 6.9% to $800.6 million in the most recent period from $748.4 million in the prior year, with operating margin at 22.1% and net income of $102.6 million. The company maintains competitive positioning through established franchise rights and a regulated utility monopoly within its approved service territories, supplemented by diversified water supply sources including groundwater, surface water, purchased water, and reclaimed water. California operations alone leverage 2,481 miles of distribution infrastructure.

Two material litigation matters warrant attention. Connecticut Water Company (CWC) faces a pending putative class action lawsuit in Connecticut Superior Court alleging that water provided by CWC contained contaminants; no financial exposure has been quantified. More significantly, SJWC and CWC are plaintiffs in a multidistrict litigation against PFAS manufacturers. Settlements have been approved with six manufacturers including Chemours, Corteva, DuPont, 3M, Tyco Fire Products, and BASF. The company received $25.1 million in 2025 and is entitled to additional proceeds from 3M distributed over an eight-year period. This settlement activity reflects the company's exposure to legacy PFAS contamination remediation costs, a theme that extends to forward capital planning.

H2O America's structural position reflects the inherent characteristics of regulated utility operations. The company is subject to rate-setting by regulators rather than market-determined pricing, constraining pricing flexibility. Operations depend heavily on water supply factors beyond management control—drought, contamination, and weather-driven demand seasonality all represent material risks. The company faces the possibility of property condemnation through eminent domain by public agencies. Compliance costs for environmental regulations, particularly PFAS treatment, represent substantial ongoing expenses. Water supply chains are geographically fragmented; California operations depend on Valley Water, Connecticut operations on the South Central Connecticut Regional Water Authority and The Metropolitan District, and Texas operations on the Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority, Lower Colorado River Authority, and West Travis County Public Utility Agency among other sources.

The company is pursuing a $540 million acquisition of Quadvest, L.P. pending completion in 2025, consisting of a $483.6 million regulated business and a $56.4 million wholesale business. Capital expenditures are planned at $458 million in the current period as part of a five-year capital plan totaling $2.568 billion. PFAS treatment capital expenditures are expected to reach approximately $400 million, and the company is advancing an Advanced Metering Infrastructure project with associated plant additions recovery through the regulatory process.

### IPAR
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/822663/000175392626000464/ipar-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed._

Interparfums Inc generates prestige fragrance products through a bifurcated structure: a 72%-owned French subsidiary (Interparfums SA) accounting for approximately 68% of net sales, and U.S.-based operations representing 32%. The company operates across 120+ countries with primary exposure to North America and Western Europe. Revenue reached $1.49 billion in 2025, up 2.5% from $1.45 billion in 2024, with gross margin of 63.6% and operating margin of 18.2%, reflecting the non-capital intensive nature of the fragrance licensing business. Interparfums positions itself around a strong brand portfolio developed through long-standing relationships with internationally renowned licensors, supported by a successful track record of product launches and a global distribution footprint.

The company disclosed a material weakness in internal controls and confirmed that disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) were not effective. This represents a structural control deficiency that investors must assess alongside the company's operational performance. Additionally, Interparfums completed a $19.7 million asset purchase from Amorepacific Europe in 2025 and has continued its M&A strategy following the 2024 Off-White brand acquisition. The company has also taken impairment charges totaling $4 million on the Rochas fashion trademark in 2024, following combined impairment charges of $9.2 million in 2021-2022, signaling ongoing challenges with certain acquired brand valuations.

Interparfums faces several structural constraints. Macy's represented 10% of net sales in 2025, elevated from 12% in 2024 but marking the first time a single customer reached that threshold, introducing retail concentration risk. The business is heavily reliant on license renewal and continuation, with no ability to control third-party manufacturers or distributors, constraining operational flexibility relative to larger competitors. Manufacturing is geographically dispersed—France and the United States serve as primary production locations, with secondary reliance on Italy, and occasional outsourcing to China, Poland, and Turkey. The company self-identifies smaller size versus major prestige fragrance competitors as a competitive disadvantage, alongside exposure to foreign currency fluctuation, seasonal demand patterns (weighted to the second half), and inflationary pressures on component costs and shipping.

Several brand initiatives are underway: Solférino is expanding to 50 doors by H1 2026 following its first boutique opening in September 2025; Goutal Paris will relaunch in 2026 with new launches in 2027; Off-White fragrance is in development for 2026 launch in 2027; Longchamp fragrance is expected to launch in 2027; and David Beckham's new signature fragrance is targeted for completion by end of 2029. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### CWT
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1035201/000162828026012444/cwt-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

California Water Service Group operates as a regulated water and wastewater utility serving approximately two million people across five western states. Revenue declined 3.5% to $1.0 billion in the most recent period, though the company maintained a gross margin of 60.9% and operating margin of 16.9%. The business segments into Water and Wastewater Services, supplying water for domestic, industrial, public, irrigation, and fire protection uses alongside wastewater collection, treatment, and recycling services. California represents 91.2% of revenue and is the primary geography, with secondary operations in Washington, Hawaii, New Mexico, and Texas. The company sources water through a combination of groundwater from adjudicated basins in California and purchased supplies from multiple municipal water agencies and districts, including the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission and Kern County Water Agency. In Texas, operations depend on a water supply agreement with the Guadalupe Blanco River Authority. The company positions itself on its established infrastructure dating to 1926, integrated service offerings, and regulatory relationships that enable rate recovery mechanisms across its footprint.

Two pending litigation matters create financial exposure. An inverse condemnation claim in the Rancho Dominguez District alleges that California Water Service Group's facilities contributed to ground oversaturation and accelerated land movement causing property damage. A second matter involves water contamination lawsuits and broader environmental and service-related litigation. Neither case has quantified financial exposure disclosed, but inverse condemnation claims can carry substantial liabilities given the potential for widespread property damages in affected areas.

The business model carries structural vulnerabilities tied to regulatory dependence and geographic concentration. California's outsized revenue share of 91.2% concentrates risk in a single state. Rate increases require regulatory commission approval and face opposition from customer advocates, with regulators setting rates independently that may not fully cover operating expenses. Water supply faces headwinds from drought and climate variability. The capital-intensive nature of the business demands significant funding—the company plans capex of $580 to $640 million, with announced initiatives including a $218 million acquisition of Nexus Nevada and Oregon water systems by end-2026, a $125 million PFAS treatment investment for six districts through 2027, and a $1.6 billion infrastructure investment proposal under its Cal Water 2024 general rate case for 2025-2027. The $45 million acquisition of remaining BVRT membership interests is expected to close in 2025.

Forward deployment includes completion of the Palos Verdes Peninsula water reliability project with anticipated rate recovery, along with the multi-year M&A and capital programs outlined above. No specific revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### WEN
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/30697/000003069726000009/wen-20251228.htm)_

Wendy's Co operates a quick-service restaurant business across three segments: U.S. company-operated and franchised locations, international operations in Canada, the United Kingdom, and 38 other foreign countries and territories, and a real estate division managing owned and leased sites plus a Canadian joint venture. The company offers hamburger sandwiches, chicken products, salads, chili, Frosty desserts, and promotional items. Revenue declined 3.1% to $2.18 billion in the most recent fiscal year, with gross margin at 13.6% and operating margin at 15.8%. Wendy's positions itself as the second largest quick-service hamburger chain in the U.S. by traffic and dollar share, competing primarily on made-to-order square hamburgers using fresh beef, menu diversity, and brand recognition and customer loyalty rather than on aggressive discounting.

The company's previous President and Chief Executive Officer departed during the fiscal year, creating a transition in top leadership. Additionally, Wendy's recorded a $12.1 million impairment of long-lived assets in the most recent fiscal year, primarily reflecting deterioration in operating performance at certain company-operated restaurants, following a $9.7 million impairment in the prior year. These consecutive impairments signal operational challenges at the company-operated restaurant base. The company also completed a $20.5 million asset purchase from franchisees during fiscal 2025.

Wendy's faces concentrated supplier risk in its core ingredients. Three independent beef processors operating five total facilities supply all fresh beef to U.S. restaurants, while six chicken processors across eleven facilities supply all chicken. One main distributor services approximately 63% of U.S. restaurants for food, packaging, and beverages, with four additional distributors covering the remaining 35%. The company acknowledges that competitors possess substantially greater financial, marketing, and advertising resources, and compete through aggressive price discounting and promotions that could apply deflationary pressure on menu pricing. Competition spans multiple channels: quick-service hamburger chains, casual dining, grocery store prepared foods, convenience outlets, and food delivery providers.

Capital expenditure is planned at $100 million to $110 million, with approximately $20 million allocated to a build-to-suit development fund in 2026. The company is advancing Project Fresh, a comprehensive plan for U.S. profitable growth, alongside digital investments and consumer-facing technology initiatives. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### BBWI
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/701985/000070198526000008/bbwi-20260131.htm)_

_Triggers: CEO changed during fiscal year._

Bath & Body Works, Inc. operates as a global leader in personal care and home fragrance products through company-owned stores, direct e-commerce, and international franchise and wholesale partnerships. The company generates revenue primarily through its Bath & Body Works segment, which encompasses body care products including fine fragrance mist, body cream, lotion, eau de parfum, body wash, hand soap, and sanitizer, alongside home fragrance offerings centered on its signature 3-wick candles. The United States and Canada represent the company's primary geographic markets, with operations spanning more than 45 additional countries. Revenue remained essentially flat at $7.3 billion, with gross margin of 43.7% and operating margin of 15.4%. The company positions itself as a market leader backed by four decades of scent expertise, an iconic brand with global recognition, a 40 million-member loyalty program, and a global footprint of 2,500 locations. A predominantly domestic, vertically-integrated supply chain and off-mall retail positioning further differentiate the business from competitors.

The company executed a CEO transition during the fiscal year, marking a leadership change that may signal strategic recalibration or operational refinement going forward. This governance shift occurs as Bath & Body Works pursues a multi-faceted transformation agenda.

Bath & Body Works operates in a highly fragmented competitive landscape encompassing specialty chains, department stores, online retailers, discount retailers, and direct marketers. The business depends on approximately 90 U.S.-based vendors for merchandise, with the largest vendor representing 12% of purchases and the five largest accounting for roughly 40% of total merchandise procurement—a concentration that carries supply continuity risk. The company explicitly discloses material structural constraints: a seasonal business in which 40% of annual sales occur in the fourth quarter; reliance on physical store locations and suitable lease space; limited control over franchise and license partners; vulnerability to mall location deterioration; and geographic concentration of manufacturing and distribution in central Ohio. These factors collectively shape earnings volatility and operational flexibility.

The company is allocating $270 million in capital expenditure and pursuing several forward initiatives: a "Consumer First Formula" transformation across brand and product, expansion of its off-mall store mix toward 75%, a February 2026 launch on Amazon in the U.S., a $250 million two-year cost savings program targeting $175 million in fiscal 2026, and an IT transformation project to enhance digital and omnichannel capabilities. Free cash flow of $865 million provides capital to support these investments.

PDF Solutions Inc operates as a single integrated business segment providing data solutions, analytics, and inspection tools to semiconductor and electronics manufacturers. Revenue grew 22% to $219.0 million in the most recent period from $179.5 million in the prior year, with gross margin expanding to 72.3%. The company's product portfolio spans characterization vehicles for parametric yield improvement, the DirectScan 3D e-beam inspection system, the Exensio data analytics and AI platform, Sapience for manufacturing process integration, Cimetrix equipment connectivity software, and the recently acquired secureWise remote connectivity offering. PDF Solutions operates primarily across the United States, Canada, China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, with secondary presence in France, Germany, and Italy.

A pending arbitration matter weighs on near-term certainty. The company won a confidential arbitration award against SMIC New Technology Research & Development (Shanghai) Corporation in November 2025 for failure to pay contract fees, but SMIC filed an application with the Hong Kong High Court in February 2026 seeking to set aside the award. Although PDF Solutions believes the set-aside application lacks merit and intends to defend and pursue judicial enforcement, no amounts have been recognized or collected as of December 31, 2025. The outcome and timing of resolution remain uncertain.

The business faces material customer concentration alongside competition from both specialized rivals and much larger incumbents. Three customers represented 53% of 2025 revenues, though concentration has shown some moderation from prior years when a single customer accounted for 35% of sales. Named competitors include large diversified equipment and software providers—KLA Corporation, Applied Materials, Synopsys, ASML—as well as internal development teams within customer organizations. PDF Solutions' stated advantages rest on demonstrated results, proprietary test structures and algorithms accumulated over 20 years, and an integrated platform spanning data collection through analytics. However, the company acknowledges dependence on a limited number of large customers, vulnerability to customer consolidation, substantial ongoing R&D requirements, reliance on sole-source specialized parts suppliers, and exposure to export controls that constrain market access.

The company completed a $130 million acquisition of SecureWise LLC in 2025 and is pursuing several integration and expansion initiatives. Key efforts include integrating SecureWise and expanding equipment data analytics, redesigning the AI-Ready Data Platform architecture to handle millions of parameters, deploying the DirectScan eProbe 450 generation tool in high-volume manufacturing, building out the Sapience Manufacturing Hub for enterprise system integration, and scaling Exensio analytics for massive dataset processing. The company is not providing revenue or earnings guidance. Operating margin stands at 14.4% despite net income of negative $600 thousand in the period.

### WLY

John Wiley & Sons operates as a global research and education publisher serving scientific, technical, medical, and scholarly audiences through two core segments. Revenue declined 10.4% to $1.68 billion in the most recent fiscal year from $1.87 billion prior year, though the company maintains a strong gross margin of 74.3% and generated $125.9 million in free cash flow. The Research segment, which includes over 1,800 scientific journals accessed through the Ayton platform serving 2,000+ publishers, and Research Solutions offerings like content platforms and recruitment services, works alongside the Learning segment covering academic and professional print and digital publishing, digital courseware, and assessments. Wiley positions itself as a predominantly digital enterprise with 83% digital revenue and holds a top-3 position in journal citations by Clarivate Analytics, supported by long-term publishing alliances with prestigious societies. The company operates primarily in the United States and United Kingdom, with secondary operations in Sri Lanka, Germany, and India.

The filing reflects a period of significant portfolio restructuring and leadership transition. The company completed multiple divestitures during 2024 and 2025, including the sale of University Services, Wiley Edge, and CrossKnowledge, culminating in the sale of Tuition Manager and other assets for $119.5 million in early 2025. These transactions were preceded by substantial goodwill impairments totaling approximately $108.4 million across the divested units in 2024, with additional held-for-sale impairments of $74.8 million reflecting downward valuations. A new CFO assumed the role during the fiscal year. These actions signal a deliberate pivot toward core research and learning publishing while exiting lower-margin or underperforming business units.

Structurally, Wiley faces competing pressures that weigh on its traditional business model. Open access mandates and transformational agreements are reshaping journal subscription revenue streams, while enrollment declines in higher education directly impact textbook and courseware demand. The company acknowledges exposure to disruption from AI technologies and unauthorized content dissemination through generative AI systems. Operating leverage remains constrained, with operating margin at 13.2%, and the company depends heavily on relationships with authors, professional societies, and subscription agents—channels where concentration risk exists. However, 48% of revenue derives from contractually obligated sources, providing revenue stability. Foreign exchange exposure is material given substantial non-US revenues.

Management has launched a Global Restructuring Program targeting $100 million in annualized cost savings, alongside enterprise modernization and cloud computing investments. Key growth initiatives focus on expanding the journal portfolio, scaling high-value digital content and assessments in Learning, and growing Open Access volumes and Transformational Agreements. No forward revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

Digi International Inc provides IoT connectivity solutions across two operating segments. Revenue grew 1.5% to $430.2 million in the twelve months ended September 30, 2025, from $424.0 million in the prior year, with gross margin of 62.9% and operating margin of 13.1%. The IoT Products & Services segment offers embedded and wireless modules, routers, infrastructure management equipment, and device management platforms to OEMs and enterprise and government customers. The IoT Solutions segment encompasses SmartSense by Digi (condition-based monitoring and task management services), the Managed Network-as-a-Service business acquired via Ventus Wireless, and Jolt Software (task management and workforce solutions). The company positions itself as a leading global provider of business and mission-critical IoT connectivity, emphasizing the strength of the Digi and XBee brand names, established carrier relationships, and product development capabilities. Operations are primarily based in the United States, with secondary international presence.

The company completed the acquisition of Jolt Software, Inc. for $145.7 million in 2025, an initiative designed to enhance SmartSense by Digi offerings and expand subscription-based solutions across the portfolio. One distributor customer of the IoT Products & Services segment represented 13% of consolidated revenue in the twelve-month period, indicating material customer concentration. Patent infringement and intellectual property claims, along with employment and customer/vendor claims, are pending. The company faces supply chain dependencies on manufacturers and component sources in Thailand, Mexico, Taiwan, and Cambodia.

Structurally, Digi operates in a competitive landscape fragmented across multiple product categories—from embedded wireless modules to enterprise WAN connectivity and managed network services. The company acknowledges that some competitors dedicate greater resources to individual product offerings, possess larger financial and technical resources, command higher brand recognition in specific geographies, and maintain longer-standing OEM relationships and larger customer bases. The company's disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting were effective as of the filing date, with no material weaknesses disclosed. Non-GAAP measures including adjusted net income, adjusted EBITDA, and annual recurring revenue (ARR) are used in reporting.

Going forward, Digi is discontinuing production of certain older IoT Products & Services products and pursuing enterprise-level deals through a direct sales model. No specific capital expenditure plans, revenue guidance, or earnings guidance were provided in the filing.

Apple Hospitality REIT, Inc. operates as a self-advised real estate investment trust focused on the lodging sector across the United States. The company owns and operates hotels under the Marriott and Hilton brand portfolios, generating revenue of $1.41 billion in the most recent period, essentially flat compared to the prior year's $1.43 billion. The business derives income from hotel rooms, food and beverage services, and other hotel-related operations. Apple Hospitality positions itself as one of the largest hospitality REITs by hotel count and guest rooms, supported by significant geographic and brand diversity. The company emphasizes its rooms-focused hotel strategy with strong operating margins of 40%, experienced asset management and operational expertise, variable management fee alignment, and low leverage that provides financial flexibility. The stated competitive advantages rest on brand recognition, customer satisfaction, and operational discipline in a fragmented market.

In April 2025, Apple Hospitality settled legal proceedings that commenced in 2024 against a third-party operator of a New York property for failure to make lease payments; the operator voluntarily surrendered possession as part of the settlement. Beyond litigation resolution, the company has been active in portfolio repositioning. During 2025, it completed acquisitions of a Homewood Suites in Tampa, Florida and a Motto property in Nashville, Tennessee, and closed the sale of five properties for $73.3 million. The company also recorded impairment losses of $5.7 million across two hotel properties in Q3 2025, following $3.1 million in impairments across three properties during 2024.

Apple Hospitality's operational structure carries inherent constraints. The company is dependent on third-party hotel managers for day-to-day operations and remains bound by franchise agreement standards and compliance costs imposed by Marriott and Hilton. Concentration risk exists in these two major brands, which form the backbone of the portfolio. Competitive pressure from market over-building in certain geographies, combined with the highly seasonal nature of the hotel industry, creates quarterly earnings volatility. The company itself acknowledges exposure to economic downturns and travel disruptions, the limited alternative uses for hotel buildings, and difficulty liquidating real estate investments quickly. These structural features define both the stability and the constraints of the REIT model.

Capital deployment plans include $80 million to $90 million in capex for 2026, with comprehensive renovation projects planned for approximately 21 properties. Additional near-term initiatives include management transitions of nine Marriott-affiliated hotels to non-affiliated operators, signaling a shift in operational strategy. Teradata Corp is a data analytics and AI software company offering cloud and on-premises solutions across two primary segments.
