The company is pursuing multiple operational initiatives: investing in R&D for new printing systems, pressure sensitive materials, scanners and software; executing tariff mitigation through price increases, sourcing adjustments and efficiency gains; and expanding sales capabilities via improved digital presence and marketing automation. Brady Corp also closed two facilities and executed associated organizational restructuring in Europe and Australia during the period. Gross margin stood at 50.3% and operating margin at 15.6%. No individual customer represents 10% or more of sales, and the company reports no single supplier dependency for most critical base materials, though some sole sourcing or limited sourcing exists for design or cost reasons. Deloitte & Touche LLP serves as auditor, and disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting are effective.

### LRN
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1157408/000155837025010334/lrn-20250630x10k.htm)_

_Triggers: none._

Stride, Inc. operates a single business segment delivering an educational platform that combines proprietary and third-party curriculum with software systems and services designed to support individualized learning. The company serves three product categories—General Education, Career Learning, and Adult Learning—with the United States representing its primary market and International generating immaterial revenue. Stride competes across a fragmented landscape that includes online curriculum providers like Pearson's Connections Academy and Edmentum, traditional textbook publishers such as McGraw Hill and Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, lower-cost digital alternatives including Khan Academy and IXL Learning, and various charter school operators and corporate training providers. The company positions itself on the strength of its virtual education expertise, comprehensive academic program suite, integrated K-12 solutions, qualified online teaching staff, and demonstrated student outcomes in math, reading, graduation, and job placement. Revenue grew 17.9% to $2.41 billion in the most recent fiscal year from $2.04 billion in the prior year, with gross margin at 39.2% and operating margin at 15.0%.

Stride completed three significant acquisitions in 2020—Galvanize, Tech Elevator, and MedCerts—substantially expanding its Career Learning and Adult Learning footprints. However, the company recorded a $59.5 million impairment of intangible assets and operating lease right-of-use assets associated with Galvanize in fiscal 2025, indicating that integration or performance of that asset fell materially short of prior expectations. The impairment suggests challenges either in sustaining the value proposition of the acquired business or in its operational integration within the broader platform.

The company's revenue model carries material structural constraints. The majority of revenues depend on per-pupil funding levels and formulas determined by state legislatures and school districts, creating revenue vulnerability to policy changes and enrollment fluctuations outside management's control. Stride operates under extensive state and federal regulation of virtual and blended public schools, faces periodic contract renewal risk, and is exposed to student withdrawal volatility. Ambiguous enabling legislation in some jurisdictions creates disputes over invoice and payment rights. The business also bears higher costs when serving academically at-risk student populations requiring supplemental support, and faces a tight labor market for state-certified teachers with specialized online instruction experience. Seasonal business fluctuations affect quarterly operating results. The competitive moat appears narrower than financial performance metrics suggest given the breadth of alternatives available to school districts and learners.

No revenue or earnings guidance was provided, and no material capital expenditure plans or strategic initiatives were disclosed. Disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting were both effective as of the filing date.

Crane NXT operates across two main segments addressing distinct but complementary markets. The company serves primary markets in the United States and United Kingdom, with secondary exposure to Mexico, Japan, Germany, Sweden, and Malta.

The company has undertaken substantial M&A activity that will shape its operations through 2026. It completed the acquisition of De La Rue Authentication Solutions for $391.1 million in 2025 and has a pending acquisition of Antares Vision S.p.A. for $137.8 million, with remaining phases expected to close through 2026 and funded via a Term Loan B facility. The De La Rue and OpSec integration is underway with restructuring continuing through 2026, creating a new Crane Authentication entity from these combined businesses. Crane NXT positions itself around proprietary and differentiated technology, particularly in advanced micro-optics for anti-counterfeiting, materials and surface technology, detection systems design, and image recognition software. A substantial portion of business operates outside the U.S., introducing currency and regulatory exposure. The company is dependent on single or sole-source suppliers for critical materials, and faces pressure from a competitive labor market. Intellectual property risk—both misappropriation and invalidation—represents a disclosed concern.

Capital expenditure is planned at $75 million to $80 million. The integration of De La Rue and Antares Vision, along with restructuring activities through 2026, will be key operational drivers. No revenue or earnings guidance has been provided.

Its stated competitive strengths center on product innovation, quality, high-reliability offerings, and in-depth process knowledge, supported by a global presence with local support capabilities. Engineering S.r.l for $16.5 million, expanding industrial dewatering and power transmission offerings. EZCORP operates a diversified pawn lending and merchandise business across the United States and Latin America. The company generated revenue of $1.13 billion in its most recent fiscal period, up 11.1% from $1.01 billion in the prior year. The business is organized into three segments: U.S. Pawn, which includes EZPAWN, Value Pawn & Jewelry and other branded operations; Latin America Pawn, operating Empeño Fácil, Cash Apoyo Efectivo and other brands across Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras; and Other Investments, which holds an equity interest in Cash Converters International Limited and investments in Founders One, LLC. Revenue streams include pawn service charges on loans, merchandise sales from pre-owned collateral and purchased goods, jewelry scrapping, product protection plans, and web-based applications through its EZ+ platform. The company positions itself as the second-largest pawn store owner and operator in the U.S. and the largest for-profit pawn operator in Guatemala, with material presence in Mexico as the second-largest for-profit operator. Its EZ+ Rewards loyalty program has reached 6.9 million global members. EZCORP competes against a broad array of participants including other pawn stores, banks, alternative lenders, credit unions, consumer finance companies, jewelry retailers, discount stores, and online merchants, emphasizing fast and simple access to cash, customer service quality, and competitive pricing.

The company's gross margin stands at 66.3% and operating margin at 13.0%, with net income of $109.6 million. The business carries identifiable structural constraints. A significant portion of U.S. operations is concentrated in Texas and Florida, creating exposure to hurricanes and tropical storms. Gold price and volume volatility directly impacts earnings. The company faces competition from larger financial institutions with substantially greater resources. Regulatory compliance costs and complexity span multiple jurisdictions. Operational risks include robberies and burglaries at store locations, and the business depends heavily on accurate collateral valuation. Additionally, the company has limited unreserved shares available for future issuance.

Looking forward, EZCORP is pursuing Latin America expansion through acquisitions and new store openings. In 2025, the company completed acquisitions of Monte Providencia and Tu Empeño Efectivo stores as well as four U.S. pawn stores. Infrastructure investments include LED lighting installation, which is now in place at 85% of U.S. stores and 60% of Latin America stores. The company is also developing IT and data modernization capabilities to support operations and the loyalty program. No revenue or earnings guidance has been provided.

### EEFT

Euronet Worldwide operates a diversified global payments platform spanning electronic funds transfer, prepaid services, and money transfer. Revenue grew 6.4% to $4.24 billion in 2025, driven by three distinct segments: Money Transfer (42% of revenues) delivers remittance and currency exchange services through Ria Money Transfer, Xe, and the Dandelion cross-border real-time payments network across 207 countries and territories; Electronic Funds Transfer (30% of revenues) manages a network of 56,818 ATMs and roughly 610,000 POS terminals offering transaction processing and value-added services; and epay (28% of revenues) operates approximately 749,000 POS terminals across 363,000 retail locations distributing prepaid mobile airtime, digital content, and gift cards. The company positions itself on the breadth of its service offerings, first-to-market digital products, and relationships with content providers and retailers. It competes globally against The Western Union Company and MoneyGram International in remittance, as well as financial institution ATM networks, national bank switches, mobile operators, and smaller local players across segments. Operating margin reached 12.5% in 2025.

Euronet completed two acquisitions in 2025 that extend its capabilities: the integration of CoreCard Corporation in October 2025 strengthens card outsourcing and issuing services, while the May 2025 equity stake acquisition in Kyodai Remittance (UNIDOS CO. LTD) establishes a foothold in Japan's remittance market. The company also incurred a $200,000 contract asset impairment in the EFT Processing Segment during 2025. These transactions reflect management's focus on expanding payment network reach and content distribution in high-growth corridors.

Euronet faces structural constraints that weigh on competitive positioning. No single customer or vendor exceeds 10% of consolidated revenues, providing diversification but also limiting negotiating leverage. The company acknowledges that competitors possess greater resources and capital access for expansion, major retailers can demand larger commission shares, and alternative technologies increasingly compete with traditional payment services. Mobile operators are expanding their own online distribution networks, and emerging market competition intensifies as those economies mature. In the remittance segment specifically, the company notes difficulty in setting competitive and profitable pricing across different payment corridors.

Capital deployment will remain material: Euronet plans capex of $135–$145 million (midpoint $140 million) in the forward period. Strategic priorities center on deploying the Ren payments platform to new markets and expanding the Dandelion cross-border real-time payments platform, signaling continued investment in real-time payment infrastructure alongside the recent CoreCard integration.

The company also recorded a $3.6 million impairment charge on machinery and equipment in fiscal 2025. The structural position reflects both concentrated customer relationships and meaningful supply chain dependencies. The company self-discloses pricing pressure from large customers, price erosion on legacy products, and dependence on timing of customer new product introductions as material disadvantages. Manufacturing and sourcing concentrate in Asia (China, Malaysia, Philippines) alongside Mexican operations, exposing the business to tariff and trade policy disruptions. Competitive positioning rests on service quality, trained technician delivery routes, and long-standing supplier relationships that secure pricing and limited access to supply. However, larger competitors with greater financial resources and broader geographic reach present ongoing pressure, and the company explicitly faces headwinds from competitive pricing dynamics, raw material volatility, and seasonal demand fluctuations in Water Treatment and agricultural products.

Acadia Realty Trust operates three interconnected segments serving the retail real estate market. Metro, Chicago, and Dallas. The Investment Management segment manages institutional co-investment vehicles (Funds II through V) that deploy capital alongside institutional partners into suburban shopping centers and urban retail assets. A Structured Financing segment originates first mortgage loans and notes receivable secured by real estate. Revenue grew 14.2% to $410.7 million in the current period from $359.7 million in the prior year, though operating margin compressed to 12.0%. This vertical integration supports active asset management through re-tenanting and property repositioning. However, the business faces material structural constraints. Geographic concentration in New York and Chicago creates meaningful portfolio risk, while dependency on anchor tenants leaves the company vulnerable to their departure. E-commerce pressure on retail demand and tenant profitability persists, illiquidity of real estate limits portfolio flexibility, and fixed costs remain regardless of revenue fluctuations. The company competes against other REITs, financial institutions, private funds, insurance companies, pension funds, and other capital sources, as well as alternative retail formats including outlet malls, discount clubs, and e-commerce retailers.

Uniti Group Inc. is a fiber infrastructure and managed services company operating across three business segments. Revenue grew 91% to $2.2 billion in the most recent period, reflecting the August 2025 completion of its merger with Windstream. Kinetic, the largest segment, provides residential and business broadband, voice, and wholesale services as an incumbent local exchange carrier across 47 states, primarily in the Midwest and Southeast, with approximately 500,000 residential fiber customers and 1.9 million fiber-equipped households. Uniti Solutions operates as a competitive local exchange carrier delivering managed services to mid-market and enterprise customers, including SD-WAN, SASE, and unified communications offerings. The Fiber Infrastructure segment provides wholesale network bandwidth, dark fiber, and colocation services to carriers, hyperscalers, and cloud providers. The company positions itself around approximately 240,000 fiber route miles of digital infrastructure and multi-gigabit fiber speeds, targeting Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets with AI-driven compute center development.

The Windstream merger fundamentally restructured Uniti's customer concentration profile. Prior to the combination, Windstream leasing revenues represented 68.3% of Old Uniti's total consolidated revenues—a substantial single-customer dependency. Following the merger's completion on August 1, 2025, no customer or related group accounts for 10% or more of consolidated revenues, eliminating that concentration risk through business integration rather than customer diversification alone. The transaction substantially expanded the company's scale, asset base, and service portfolio in a single event.

Uniti faces material competitive headwinds that directly constrain its market position. The company discloses that approximately 20% of its footprint operates without a high-speed wireline competitor, but notes that very few locations lack meaningful competition entirely—a narrow margin of competitive moat. Cable operators face less stringent regulatory requirements than Kinetic in many jurisdictions. Wireless home internet adoption is accelerating among consumers, while satellite broadband offerings have improved in rural and lower-speed copper areas. The company also depends on other carriers for network capacity in certain markets where those carriers compete directly—a structural dependency risk. High debt levels require substantial ongoing cash flow allocation for interest and principal payments. Operating margin stands at 11.7%, modest for an infrastructure business, reflecting the competitive intensity and capital intensity of the sector.

The company has identified multiple growth drivers for the forward period. A multi-year AI infrastructure build program targeting high-count dark fiber deployment is underway, aligned with broader demand for compute center connectivity. Kinetic is expanding its fiber footprint to 1.9 million premises with a target penetration rate of 41%. The company received $184.3 million in BEAD broadband funding awards covering 58,000 locations, providing external capital support for rural expansion. A Kinetic asset-backed securitization program closed in Q1 2026 with a $960.1 million offering, supporting balance sheet flexibility.

No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### USPH
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/885978/000114036126007170/ef20060831_10k.htm)_

_Triggers: none._

U.S. Physical Therapy operates a geographically diversified network of outpatient therapy clinics and industrial services across 44 states, with material presence in Texas, Tennessee, Michigan, and New York. The company comprises two segments: Physical Therapy Operations, which delivers physical, speech, and occupational therapy services alongside home-care practices focused on orthopedic and sports-related injuries; and Industrial Injury Prevention Services (IIP), which provides onsite employer-contracted services including injury prevention, performance optimization, functional capacity evaluations, and ergonomic assessments. Revenue grew 16.3% to $781 million in the most recent period from $671 million, with gross margin of 19.2% and operating margin of 11.1%. The company positions itself as one of the largest national outpatient physical therapy providers by combining local clinic identity with national purchasing power, centralized management practices, and standardized processes across a therapist-owner partnership model.

The company has pursued an aggressive acquisition strategy across three years. In 2024 alone, USPH deployed approximately $144.8 million in acquisitions, including a $76.5 million investment for 50% of Metro and $24 million for the IIP business through Briotix Health. In 2025, it completed three additional physical therapy practice acquisitions totaling $26.6 million, along with a $2.3 million home-care practice acquisition. The company is also executing a strategic hospital alliance in New York with 60 clinics expected to be operational by year-end 2026 and implementing an ERP system for human resources and accounting functions. A $2.4 million impairment of assets held for sale in fiscal 2024 suggests some integration or divestiture activity alongside the broader M&A agenda.

U.S. Physical Therapy carries structural headwinds that shape its risk profile. The business is heavily dependent on Medicare reimbursement rates subject to frequent regulatory changes and faces reliance on third-party payor approvals in certain markets. Labor costs represent the largest operating expense with competitive wage pressures, and the company depends on maintaining physician relationships for referrals. It is also subject to post-payment audits with potential for retroactive payment reductions and faces state-specific corporate practice of medicine and fee-splitting restrictions. Competition spans hospital physical therapy departments, private clinics, physician-owned practices, chiropractors, and large rehabilitation entities with potentially superior resources. The company has disclosed exposure to regulatory investigations and compliance costs as a material disadvantage.

The company is expanding through both organic network development and acquisition integration, with the New York hospital alliance and Metro home-care expansion forming near-term growth vectors. No specific revenue or earnings guidance has been provided, and no capex figures are disclosed. Disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting are effective, and the auditor is Grant Thornton LLP with no recent leadership changes.

### SMPL
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1702744/000170274425000046/atk-20250830.htm)_

_Triggers: none._

Simply Good Foods Co operates across two integrated operating segments—Quest and Atkins, and OWYN—aggregated into a single reportable segment due to their aligned financial and operational characteristics. The company develops, markets, and sells nutritional snacking products positioned around protein-rich, low-carb, and low-sugar formulations. Its product portfolio spans protein bars, ready-to-drink protein shakes, salty snacks (protein chips and crackers), baked goods, confections, protein powders, iced coffee beverages, and recipes. Revenue grew 9% to $1.45 billion in the most recent fiscal year from $1.33 billion prior year, with gross margin of 36.2% and operating margin of 10.8%. North America is the primary geography, with secondary operations in Australia and New Zealand. The company positions itself as a leader in the nutritional snacking category, leveraging brand strength in Quest, Atkins, and OWYN, prominent retailer shelf positioning in nutrition and wellness aisles, and alignment with consumer trends toward protein and low-sugar products.

The company completed its acquisition of Only What You Need, Inc. (the OWYN brand) for $281.9 million in June 2024, expanding its plant-based product capabilities. In the current fiscal year, Simply Good Foods recorded impairment charges against both the Atkins brand and trademarks (an indefinite-lived intangible asset) and certain licensing agreement agreements (finite-lived intangible assets), signaling pressure on the Atkins business line. Management has disclosed a strategic repositioning of the Atkins brand distribution for fiscal 2026, acknowledging reduction in retailer shelf space and points of distribution. These dynamics underscore near-term headwinds in a legacy brand even as the company pursues broader initiatives: product line extensions and innovation across Quest and OWYN, e-commerce expansion, and marketing targeting GLP-1 medication users.

The business carries material customer concentration risk, with Walmart Inc. (across mass retail, Sam's Club, and e-commerce channels) and Amazon together representing 49% of sales. The company relies on a limited number of contract manufacturers for production, creating supply-chain vulnerability. Competitive pressure stems from multinational, regional, and local packaged food producers, private label offerings, and companies focused on specific dietary approaches (keto, paleo, vegan, gluten-free). While the company cites an asset-light model, proven brand-building track record, rapid product development, and an experienced leadership team as advantages, it acknowledges competitors with substantially greater financial resources, broader product ranges, and lower-cost alternatives. The Atkins brand erosion noted above exemplifies this competitive dynamic.

No forward revenue, earnings, or capex guidance was provided. The company maintains effective disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, with no restatement, going-concern, or material weakness disclosures. Deloitte & Touche LLP serves as auditor.

### CNK
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1385280/000119312526056015/cnk-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: none._

Cinemark Holdings, Inc. operates as a theatrical exhibition company with a geographically diversified footprint spanning North America and Latin America. The company generated $3.12 billion in revenue in fiscal 2025, up 2.1% from $3.05 billion in the prior year. Cinemark's U.S. segment comprises 303 theaters with 4,241 screens across 42 states, while its international operations span 193 theaters and 1,396 screens across 13 Latin American countries, with Brazil and Argentina serving as primary markets alongside secondary exposure to Colombia, Chile, Peru, and Central America. Revenue flows from four categories: admissions, concession, screen advertising, and other sources. The company positions itself on several competitive strengths: the largest exhibitor-branded premium large format footprint with 301 XD auditoriums, leading market share in most U.S. markets served, market-leading positions in Brazil and Argentina, over 27 million members in global loyalty programs, and a sophisticated technology platform supporting omni-channel marketing. Operating margin reached 10.7% in the period.

Cinemark faces headwinds rooted in structural shifts in content availability and competitive dynamics. The company explicitly identifies reduced volume of new film releases and weaker film performance as material disadvantages, alongside shorter and more variable theatrical windows that compress box office potential. Currency fluctuations and foreign exchange risks in Latin American operations represent ongoing exposure, and the company carries significant long-term debt and lease obligations that constrain financial flexibility. Supply chain interruptions and inflationary pressures on concession costs add operational friction. Within its theater base, Cinemark recorded $6.5 million in impairments during fiscal 2025 related to underperformance at four domestic theaters and 13 international locations, with an additional $1.5 million impairment the prior year tied to a Latin American theater's incomplete recovery post-COVID reopening.

Competitive pressure emanates from multiple directions. Named direct competitors include Regal, AMC, Cinépolis, Cine Colombia, CinePlanet, Kinoplex (GSR), UCI, Royal Films, and Araujo. Beyond traditional exhibitors, Cinemark competes against dine-in theaters, tavern-style theaters, family entertainment centers, and out-of-home venues spanning concerts, theme parks, gaming, and sports. The broader competitive set includes streaming services, digital downloads, video-on-demand, and network television as alternative film distribution channels.

Cinemark plans capital expenditures of $219 million, with initiatives centered on venue modernization and technology enhancement. The company is executing a multi-year laser projector conversion project targeting 22% completion, converting auditoriums to energy-efficient Barco RGB laser systems. Luxury Lounger heated recliner seats are being expanded to additional locations, and mobile concession ordering is expanding across U.S. and Latin American theaters. The company has signed new build and expansion commitments totaling $74.6 million. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### KBH
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795266/000079526626000017/kbh-20251130.htm)_

KB Home is a homebuilder operating across four regional segments—West Coast (California, Idaho, Washington), Southwest (Arizona, Nevada), Central (Colorado, Texas), and Southeast (Florida, North Carolina)—plus a Financial Services division providing insurance, title, and mortgage banking through KBHS. The company builds attached and detached single-family homes, townhomes, condominiums, and active adult communities, positioning itself toward first-time, move-up, and active adult buyers. Revenue declined 10% to $6.24 billion in fiscal 2025 from $6.93 billion in the prior year, with gross margin contracting to 18.6% and operating margin at 8.2%. California is the primary geography by materiality, with Arizona, Nevada, Colorado, Texas, and Florida as secondary markets.

KB Home's competitive positioning centers on its Built to Order model, which the company emphasizes as delivering personalized homebuying experience and high customer satisfaction. The company touts energy-efficient and water-saving homes, standardized floor plans that reduce construction costs, a pre-sold homes backlog that lowers financing risk, and industry-leading sustainability certifications. However, the company discloses material structural constraints: high concentration in California, Florida, Nevada, and Texas creates geographic risk; rising land acquisition and development costs are pressuring margins; supply chain disruptions and material cost inflation persist; contractor availability remains constrained; and tariffs on imported materials add cost pressure. The company also faces competition from larger homebuilders with greater resources and dependence on third-party mortgage lenders and GR Alliance performance. During fiscal 2025, KB Home took $15.5 million in inventory impairments on four communities and land parcels, driven by increased municipal land development costs and strategic operational changes to accelerate monetization.

The company is guiding fiscal 2026 revenue to a range of $5.1 billion to $6.1 billion, representing a lowered outlook from prior expectations, with midpoint guidance at $5.6 billion. Key initiatives include increasing Built to Order homes to 60–70% of the delivery mix (from 55% in 2025), expanding land and land development investments in attractive submarkets, continuing share repurchases of $50–100 million in Q1 2026, and selectively expanding wildfire resilience community standards in 2026 following the March 2025 launch of the nation's first new-home community meeting IBHS wildfire resilience standards. No capex figures are provided in forward guidance.

### NABL

N-able, Inc. provides unified endpoint management, security operations, and data protection solutions designed for IT services providers and their customers. The company generated $511.4 million in revenue in the most recent period, representing 9.7% growth from $466.1 million in the prior year. Operating as a single reporting unit, N-able serves the United States, United Kingdom, and international markets with a platform that integrates endpoint management, data protection as-a-service, security operations, and business management capabilities. The company maintains a gross margin of 77.1%, though operating margin of 7.2% reflects execution costs across its go-to-market and product development functions.

N-able positions itself as purpose-built for managed service provider success, emphasizing centralized visibility and control, flexible subscription pricing, and efficient deployment at scale. The company distinguishes itself through comprehensive platform integration with third-party tools and best-in-class partner support strategies. It completed the acquisition of Adlumin, Inc. in 2024 to integrate extended detection and response capabilities, and previously acquired Spinpanel B.V. in 2022. Current strategic initiatives focus on expanding long-term committed contracts, integrating the Adlumin acquisition, growing the channel partner base globally, and enhancing security service offerings and automation.

N-able faces a fragmented competitive landscape populated by both pure-play MSP vendors—including ConnectWise, Kaseya, and NinjaOne—and category-specific competitors spanning data protection (Acronis, Veeam), managed detection and response (ArcticWolf), endpoint protection (Sophos), and remote access (TeamViewer, LogMeIn). The company's stated disadvantages include substantial indebtedness that limits financial flexibility, dependence on channel partners for customer acquisition and retention, exposure to foreign exchange fluctuations, and reliance on third-party cloud infrastructure providers. Larger competitors and market fragmentation present ongoing competitive headwinds.

The company disclosed no revenue or earnings per share guidance, capex plans, or material litigation or regulatory actions in this filing. Disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting are effective, with no material weaknesses identified and no restatements or going concern issues mentioned.

ePlus Inc operates as an integrated IT solutions provider across four primary segments: Product (hardware, software, and supply chain solutions), Professional Services (consulting, deployment, and logistics), Managed Services (security, cloud, and service desk offerings), and Financing (equipment leases and consumption-based arrangements). Revenue declined 7% to $2.07 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, with gross margin at 27.5% and operating margin at 6.8%. The company positions itself as a leading provider spanning security, cloud, data center, networking, collaboration, and artificial intelligence, supported by advanced professional services and proprietary cloud-based supply chain software. The U.S. represents its primary geographic market, with secondary operations in the United Kingdom, European Union, India, and Singapore.

A significant restructuring effort is underway following two acquisitions in 2024: Bailiwick Services for $124.9 million in August 2024, and Peak Resources. Concurrent with these additions, the company is expanding its AI advisory services capabilities, including a Secure GenAI Accelerator offering, and building out its Cloud Managed Services portfolio. An ePlus AI Experience Center has been established to address data center AI infrastructure needs. These initiatives reflect a strategic pivot toward higher-margin services and emerging technologies, likely undertaken to counteract the revenue contraction evident in the current-year results.

ePlus faces structural headwinds that warrant investor attention. Verizon Communications represented 16% of net sales in the current fiscal year, down from 19% and 22% in the prior two years—a positive sign of customer diversification, though still a material concentration. The company depends heavily on three distributors (Ingram Micro, Arrow Electronics, and TD SYNNEX) for over 25% of product segment purchases. Competitive pressures are acute: the company acknowledges that some rivals possess greater financial resources and operating histories, can respond faster to new opportunities, benefit from stronger brand recognition, and compete aggressively on pricing. OEMs themselves are launching managed and adoption services to lock in customer relationships. In financing, competitors with deeper capital access and better positioning for interest rate volatility pose a direct challenge to that segment's origination volumes.

The company carries internal constraints as well. Several competitors are larger with greater resources for technology investment; some can offer more attractive commercial terms; direct marketers undercut on price with minimal value-add. ePlus disclosed no material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting, and disclosure controls remain effective. However, the 7% revenue decline and 6.8% operating margin—relatively thin—suggest execution risk as the company integrates recent acquisitions and pivots toward services and AI-oriented offerings. No revenue or earnings guidance has been provided for forward periods.

Progyny, Inc. operates a purpose-built platform delivering women's health and family building benefits solutions to employers in the United States. Revenue grew 10.4% to $1.29 billion, reflecting expansion of its integrated fertility, pharmacy, pregnancy, postpartum, and menopause offerings. The company structures its business around seven product categories: a core Fertility Benefits Solution anchored by its Smart Cycle plan design, Progyny Rx (pharmacy benefits), Pregnancy and Postpartum, Menopause and Midlife, Benefit and Leave Navigation, Parent and Child Wellbeing, and Progyny Global services. The company positions itself on superior clinical outcomes—higher live birth rates and lower miscarriage rates—backed by a selective network of 1,100+ fertility specialists and high-touch member support through Progyny Care Advocates. It competes against health insurance companies offering fertility management, specialty providers backed by insurance carriers or private equity, and fertility-focused PBMs, claiming advantages in data-driven continuous improvement and comprehensive, unlimited treatment access across all employee groups.

Progyny completed two acquisitions during this period: Apryl GmbH in 2024 and Benefit Bump LLC in 2025, signaling expansion of its solution suite beyond core fertility benefits. These acquisitions align with stated initiatives to broaden addressable market reach and deepen integrated offerings in adjacent women's health categories.

The business operates with distinctive structural characteristics shaped by its market position and regulatory environment. Gross margin of 23.6% and operating margin of 6.6% reflect the high-touch service model and selective provider network that differentiate the platform. The company discloses material dependencies on benefits consultants and referrals from existing clients for customer acquisition, and notes seasonality with revenue concentrated in the second half of the year. Stated disadvantages include exposure to changing reproductive rights laws and abortion restrictions—a sector-specific regulatory risk—alongside standard PBM regulatory pressures around transparency and rebate practices. The company also acknowledges limited operating history with its current integrated platform and inherent difficulty predicting member utilization rates, which creates revenue volatility risk.

Forward initiatives center on market expansion and product penetration. Progyny targets large group fully insured employers with 2,500+ covered lives as a new addressable segment, aims to achieve 97% Progyny Rx adoption across new clients in 2025, and plans incremental Smart Cycle expansion alongside rollout of pregnancy, postpartum, and menopause solutions. No specific revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### WD

Walker & Dunlop operates as a commercial real estate finance and services platform serving the U.S. market primarily through three segments. Capital Markets provides Agency lending, debt brokerage, property sales, appraisal and valuation services, and investment banking advisory. Servicing & Asset Management handles loan portfolio servicing from Agency and principal lending activities while managing third-party capital in commercial real estate and affordable housing funds. The company positions itself as one of the largest multifamily service providers in the country, claims technology and brand advantages, and holds approval as one of 25 Fannie Mae DUS lenders and one of 23 Freddie Mac lenders nationwide. Revenue grew 9% to $1.23 billion in the most recent period from $1.13 billion prior year, though operating margin remained thin at 6.4% with net income of $56.2 million.

The filing reflects material headwinds in the affordable housing segment. Walker & Dunlop recorded $26.1 million in investment impairments at LIHTC subsidiaries due to continuing underperformance, a $13.6 million real estate held-for-use impairment at an LIHTC subsidiary, and a $7.5 million accrual for expected losses on disposition of certain affordable assets in fiscal 2025. Additionally, a $33 million goodwill impairment related to the GeoPhy reporting unit was recorded in 2024, attributed to sustained challenging macroeconomic conditions and declined projected cash flows. The company completed acquisition of the remaining 25% interest in Zelman & Associates during 2024.

The competitive position carries structural constraints. Walker & Dunlop acknowledges that many competitors possess greater name recognition and financial resources, well-established investment management platforms, and access to lower-cost capital. Large national commercial banks hold inherent advantages through existing borrower relationships. The company's performance depends materially on multifamily sector conditions, on continued approval and support from Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and HUD/Ginnie Mae programs, and on macroeconomic stability—the filing notes that macroeconomic disruption since 2022 materially disrupted transaction activity. The affordable housing business, where the company positions itself as the ninth largest LIHTC syndicator, operates in a fragmented industry and has proven vulnerable to valuation pressures and asset underperformance. A London office opening and technology infrastructure scaling represent geographic and operational expansion efforts.

Forward plans include raising and deploying capital through Debt Fund II for transitional multifamily lending, increasing GSE lending capacity to $176 billion in 2026, and expanding LIHTC syndication and affordable housing services. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

LA-Z-BOY INC operates as a vertically integrated furniture manufacturer, wholesaler, and retailer with a dual business model. Revenue grew 3% to $2.1 billion in the most recent fiscal year. The Retail segment comprises 203 company-owned La-Z-Boy Furniture Galleries stores selling upholstered furniture, casegoods, and accessories to end consumers. The Wholesale segment manufactures and imports furniture under five brands—La-Z-Boy, England, American Drew, Hammary, and Kincaid—distributing through proprietary galleries, Comfort Studio operators, major dealers, and independent retailers. The company's product portfolio spans recliners, motion furniture, sofas, sectionals, and wood casegoods including bedroom and dining sets. Geographic reach extends across the United States, Canada, and Mexico as primary markets, with secondary operations in the United Kingdom, Australia, China, New Zealand, Thailand, and Hong Kong, plus roughly 50 other countries. The company positions itself as the leading global producer of reclining chairs, one of the largest manufacturers and distributors of residential furniture in the US, and the third largest retailer of single-branded furniture nationally. Stated competitive advantages include brand heritage, an extensive proprietary retail network, customization capabilities, vertical integration, and design services.

LA-Z-BOY wrote down $20.6 million in goodwill tied to its United Kingdom reporting unit and impaired $2.1 million in long-lived assets there during fiscal 2025, reflecting operational underperformance in that geography. In the same period, the company completed four acquisitions of retail businesses across the United States—located in Davenport, Iowa; Melbourne and Cocoa, Florida; Toledo, Ohio; and Lansing and Portage, Michigan—signaling continued consolidation of independent dealers into the proprietary store network.

The company faces material structural constraints. Polyurethane foam is sourced from only three suppliers. Over 90% of imported finished goods originate from Vietnam, with roughly half concentrated among three major suppliers. Cover materials—fabrics and leather—come from a limited set of major suppliers, with raw-state sourcing spanning China, Brazil, and Vietnam; cut-and-sew operations depend on Mexico. Wholesale revenues depend on approximately 60% proprietary channel sales, 10% from large regional dealers, and 30% from other independent retailers. Operating margin stands at 6.4%, which reflects the capital intensity and operational overhead of maintaining a large physical retail footprint while competing against online retailers, direct-to-consumer brands, foreign manufacturers, big box retailers, and digital-only competitors. The company explicitly discloses disadvantages including exposure to tariffs on imported goods, vulnerability to raw material price swings, difficulty fully passing cost increases to customers, and dependence on physical store sales despite a stated headwind of shifting consumer preference toward online purchasing.

LA-Z-BOY plans capital expenditures of $90 million to $100 million in fiscal 2026. Growth initiatives include opening 13 to 18 new La-Z-Boy Furniture Galleries stores and relocating or remodeling 20 to 25 existing locations; opening or updating approximately 80 Comfort Studio locations; opening over 300 La-Z-Boy branded space locations; advancing profitable growth of the Joybird brand through small-format stores and digital expansion; and redesigning the manufacturing and distribution network for supply chain optimization.

Tennant Co operates as a single segment manufacturer and servicer of nonresidential surface maintenance equipment, generating revenue of $1.2 billion in the most recent period, down 6.5% from $1.3 billion in the prior year. The company designs, manufactures, and sells manual and autonomous mechanized cleaning equipment alongside detergent-free and other sustainable cleaning technologies, aftermarket parts and consumables, equipment maintenance and repair services, and business solutions including financing, rental, leasing, and asset management offerings. Tennant maintains a balanced geographic footprint across the Americas, Europe Middle East and Africa, and Asia Pacific regions. The business operates under structural pressures that merit scrutiny. The company relies on sole-source vendors in portions of its supply chain, heightening vulnerability to component shortages and disruptions. Labor shortages and wage inflation present ongoing cost pressures. Gross margin stood at 40.2% with operating margin at only 5.7%—relatively thin for a branded equipment manufacturer—reflecting both the revenue contraction and underlying margin compression from cost inflation and pricing constraints. Net income of $43.8 million on $1.2 billion in revenue underscores the leverage impact of operating challenges.

Tennant is executing a multiyear North America ERP system stabilization program through mid-2026, an initiative expected to absorb management attention through that horizon. The company is pursuing expansion of its robotics portfolio and autonomous solutions, supply chain resilience through regional manufacturing strategies, and pricing and cost-management initiatives designed to offset tariff impacts. No specific revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

Gentherm Inc operates in two distinct segments: Automotive, which designs and manufactures climate control seats, climate control interiors, lumbar and massage comfort solutions, and valve systems for global vehicle manufacturers; and Medical, which produces patient temperature management systems for therapeutic applications in intensive care and surgical settings. Financially, Gentherm's margins remain compressed. Gross margin stands at 24.2%, while operating margin is 5.5%—both thin for a tier-one automotive supplier, reflecting the structural cost pressures embedded in customer contracts and competitive dynamics. The company derives meaningful revenue from two named customers, Lear Corporation and Adient plc, creating customer concentration risk, though no specific threshold percentages are disclosed. The Medical segment is smaller but growing, with new product launches assumed to drive 14% revenue growth in that unit.

Gentherm has announced a reverse Morris trust merger with Modine Manufacturing Company's Performance Technologies subsidiary, expected to close in Q4 2026. The company plans capital expenditures in the $45 million to $55 million range and is executing a global manufacturing footprint optimization restructuring in Europe and Asia. The competitive landscape presents structural headwinds specific to Veeco's position. The company faces competitors with greater financial and engineering resources, and encounters systematic disadvantages tied to its U.S. location: tariffs on overseas-sourced materials are expected to increase costs, while foreign competitors with manufacturing operations outside the U.S. benefit from a more favorable tariff environment. Veeco discloses reliance on certain principal customers for a significant portion of sales without specifying thresholds. The company also faces presumption of denial for export licenses to certain China customers and military end users, and acknowledges a disadvantage relative to non-U.S. competitors in export restriction enforcement. Local manufacturers in foreign countries may receive preference due to nationalism and local policies. Chinese state-owned and affiliated entities receiving substantial government investment represent another competitive pressure point.

Veeco completed the acquisition of Epiluvac AB in 2023 but recorded a $28.1 million impairment of intangible assets from that deal in fiscal 2024 due to SiC technology market penetration falling short of expectations. The company is pursuing a merger with Axcelis Technologies pending regulatory approval. Active product initiatives include nanosecond annealing system evaluation at Tier 1 logic customers, ion beam deposition 300 system evaluation at DRAM customers, and revenue growth anticipated from its Propel 300mm GaN on Silicon platform in the second half of 2026. Veeco is also expanding its IBD-EUV technology into the EUV pellicles business. No revenue or earnings guidance has been provided.

### DLX
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/27996/000002799626000037/dlx-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: none._

Deluxe Corp operates across four business segments serving North American markets. Revenue was essentially flat at $2.13 billion in the most recent fiscal year, up just 0.5% from the prior year, with gross margin at 53% and operating margin at 5.3%. The company's Merchant Services segment provides in-store, online, and mobile payment solutions for accepting electronic payments. B2B Payments offers treasury management solutions including automated receivables technology, lockbox processing, remote deposit capture, and integrated accounts payable disbursements. Data Solutions delivers data-driven marketing analytics and services alongside web-based offerings such as financial institution profitability reporting and business incorporation services. The Print segment manufactures checks, business forms, and promotional products including branded apparel and digital storefront solutions.

Deluxe completed an asset purchase from JPMorgan Chase Bank for $24.6 million in 2025 aimed at scaling its B2B Payments business. The company also announced an asset sale for $25 million expected in 2026 and took a $5.7 million impairment charge related to exiting a joint venture for a business payment distribution technology platform during the fiscal year. These moves reflect active portfolio management as the company reshapes its operations around growth areas.

The company's competitive position reflects both structural strengths and secular headwinds. Deluxe cites a skilled workforce with industry tenure, solid infrastructure and partnerships, fully digital customer onboarding, ownership of core payment technology including gateways and risk management, extensive proprietary data assets, established relationships with financial institutions, and digital print-on-demand manufacturing capabilities. However, the business faces fundamental headwinds: check usage has declined steadily since the mid-1990s, demand for business forms continues to erode, and the payments landscape remains highly competitive with continuous innovation pressure. Rising material costs, particularly for paper—sourced over 95% from Forest Stewardship Council-certified mills—create margin pressure alongside pricing pressure from financial institutions. The company also carries exposure to interest rate risk on variable-rate debt and vulnerability to small business spending during economic slowdowns. The competitive set spans fintech firms, independent payment processors, credit card processors, treasury service providers, advertising agencies, marketing technology firms, check printing software vendors, office supply retailers, and online printing companies.

Deluxe plans capital expenditures in the $90 million to $100 million range. Key initiatives include integrating the JPMorgan Chase CheckMatch acquisition to drive B2B Payments scale, advancing data analytics and digital capabilities, expanding in high-growth verticals and markets, and continuing balance sheet strengthening through debt reduction. Free cash flow in the most recent period was $175.3 million.

Revenue grew 14.1% to $795 million in fiscal 2025 from $696 million in the prior year, with gross margin of 54.1% and operating margin of 5.0%.

Q2 took a software impairment charge in fiscal 2025 on certain capitalized software development costs no longer expected to be recoverable, though no amount was specified in the filing. The company also reoccupied part of a previously vacated facility lease during the year. These items suggest asset write-downs related to development efforts and a modest shift in real estate footprint, though neither appears to have been disclosed as material litigation or a regulatory action.

However, Q2 acknowledges material structural headwinds: larger, better-resourced competitors; customer reluctance to migrate from legacy systems; sales cycles extending 6 to 9+ months; dependency on AWS and Microsoft Azure for cloud infrastructure; and a limited patent portfolio. ### CERT

Certara, Inc. provides biosimulation science, technology, and consulting services to the biopharmaceutical and biotech industry under a single operating segment focused on Model-Informed Drug Development (MIDD). The company offers software licenses and subscriptions, technology-enabled services, professional services, and specialized solutions including an empirical biosimulation software platform, scientific informatics for drug discovery, preclinical and clinical data automation, and regulatory science tools. Revenue grew 8.7% to $418.8 million in the most recent fiscal year, with gross margin of 61.5%, though operating margin remains compressed at 5.0% and the company reported net income of negative $1.6 million. Certara operates primarily in the United States with secondary presence in Europe, Asia, and 28 countries globally.

The company has pursued an acquisition strategy to expand its platform capabilities. In 2024, Certara acquired Chemaxon, Kft. for $96.4 million to integrate drug discovery informatics. In 2023, the company completed three acquisitions: Applied BioMath for $36.6 million, Formedix Limited for $41.4 million, and Drug Interaction Solutions from the University of Washington for $8.3 million. These transactions reflect effort to build an integrated end-to-end platform. However, a $47.0 million goodwill impairment charge was recorded in fiscal 2023 related to the regulatory writing reporting unit, which was subsequently integrated into the CDDS segment, signaling challenges in realizing expected value from prior acquisitions in that area.

Certara's customer base is not heavily concentrated, with no single customer accounting for more than 10% of revenues and the ten largest customers representing 24% of total revenues. The competitive landscape is fragmented, with Certara competing against both established technology firms such as Mathworks, Dassault Systemes, and Ansys, as well as specialized biosimulation vendors including Simulations Plus, NONMEM, and others. The company also faces competition from open-source solutions, internally developed software within biopharmaceutical companies, and clinical research organizations. Certara positions itself on the combination of scientific expertise, regulatory relationships, validated modeling platforms, and breadth across molecular types and therapeutic areas—noting that 90% of FDA novel drug approvals used customer solutions. The stated disadvantages include customer preference for status quo methods, consolidation in the biopharmaceutical industry reducing customer base and increasing pricing pressure, and the emerging threat of AI-driven competitors operating at lower cost.

Forward initiatives include the Phoenix Cloud AI PK reports module launch, Pinnacle 21 Enterprise Plus release, Certara IQ next-generation quantitative systems pharmacology platform, and CoAuthor regulatory writing software with generative AI capabilities. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided. Disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting are effective, with RSM US LLP serving as auditor.

### WS

Worthington Steel operates as a value-added steel processor across North America and select international markets. Revenue declined 9.8% to $3.09 billion in the most recent fiscal year from $3.43 billion previously, with gross margin compressing to 12.6%. The company operates through a single Steel Processing segment that handles flat-rolled steel processing, electrical steel laminations, tailor welded blanks, and flat-rolled steel coils. It positions itself around market-leading positions in North American carbon flat-rolled steel and tailor welded blanks, plus standing as one of the largest global producers of electrical steel laminations. The company emphasizes 70 years of processing capability, customization capacity, and service reach across the United States, Canada, and Mexico as primary markets, with secondary operations in Germany, China, and India. An advantaged cost structure and flexible operating footprint allow it to serve diverse end markets and scale between direct and tolling services.

The company executed two acquisitions in fiscal 2024–2025: the completion of a controlling stake in Sitem Group (Italy) and the $21 million acquisition of Voestalpine Nagold in 2024. Worthington also announced several facility initiatives, including expansion of electrical steel operations in Mexico to serve the automotive market and in Canada to serve the transformer market, plus construction of a new manufacturing facility in Burlington, Ontario. In the same period, the company consolidated its Cleveland, Ohio toll processing facility into its Twinsburg, Ohio facility, generating a $6.1 million impairment charge. Additionally, Worthington recognized a $1.3 million full impairment of an indefinite-lived in-process research and development asset at its tailor welded blanks division due to inability to commercialize the underlying technology.

The structural position carries significant customer concentration risk: the automotive industry accounts for 52% of net sales, with the Detroit Three automakers alone representing 33% of consolidated revenue. The company sources flat-rolled steel coils primarily from North American mills, creating supply chain dependency. Operating margin of 4.8% reflects the highly competitive and fragmented nature of steel processing, where the company faces exposure to raw material price volatility and difficulty passing cost increases to customers in competitive conditions. Stated disadvantages include vulnerability to inventory holding losses during declining steel prices and cyclical demand in automotive and construction segments. Competition comes from domestic and foreign processors, subsidized foreign producers, and alternative material suppliers including aluminum, cement, wood, and composites.

The company is pursuing electrical steel capacity expansion in Mexico and Canada alongside the new Burlington facility construction to position for future demand. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### ASTE

Astec Industries manufactures heavy equipment for infrastructure and materials processing, organized into two segments. Infrastructure Solutions designs and produces asphalt plants, concrete plants, road construction equipment, industrial thermal systems, and recycling equipment, along with industrial automation controls and telematics platforms. Materials Solutions manufactures crushing, screening, washing, and material handling equipment for aggregate and minerals processing, and provides aftermarket servicing and parts. The company operates primarily in the United States and Canada, with secondary operations in Brazil, South Africa, India, China, and the United Kingdom. Revenue grew 8.1% to $1.41 billion in the most recent fiscal year, though gross margin remains compressed at 26.5% and operating margin stands at 4.7%.

Astec completed two acquisitions during this period: TerraSource Holdings, LLC for $252.6 million in 2025, and CWMF, LLC in January 2026. These additions expand the Materials Solutions segment and extend the company's product reach in crushing and screening. The company recorded a $20.2 million goodwill impairment for the Materials Solutions reporting unit in fiscal 2024, suggesting integration or valuation challenges in that segment. The company is in the middle stages of ERP implementation expected to conclude in 2028 or 2029, a multi-year systems transition that will require ongoing capital and management focus.

Astec operates in a fragmented competitive landscape facing both smaller domestic and international manufacturers as well as larger players with greater financial resources—including Caterpillar, Wirtgen Group, Terex Corporation, and others. The company's stated advantages include patented warm mix asphalt technology, portable asphalt and concrete plants, industry-leading jaw crushers and screening equipment, and a connected digital asset base. However, structural vulnerabilities are material. Fixed costs cannot be quickly reduced during demand downturns, and the business faces cyclical construction equipment demand. Supply chain risk is acute: the company relies on limited suppliers for steel and components with extended lead times, and faces exposure to steel tariffs. Competition from larger, better-capitalized competitors constrains pricing power. The company also carries execution risk from innovation initiatives with potential for negative margins and complexity around integrating acquisitions to realize intended synergies.

Capital expenditure is planned at $45 million, within a $40 million to $50 million range, supporting the ERP implementation, TerraSource integration, and expansion of the Astec Digital ecosystem. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided for forward periods.

### LGIH

LGI Homes, Inc. constructs and sells entry-level and active adult homes across seven regional segments spanning the West, Northwest, Central, Midwest, Florida, Southeast, and Mid-Atlantic. The company operates through multiple product lines including attached and detached entry-level homes, active adult communities, luxury homes under its Terrata Homes brand, wholesale homes, and single-family rental properties. Primary markets are Texas, Arizona, Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina, with secondary operations across California, Washington, Colorado, and other regional markets. The company positions itself on experienced management since the mid-1990s, over 80,000 homes constructed and closed since 2003, flexible land acquisition strategy targeting locations outside dense urban centers, and a customer-centric sales approach. Revenue declined 22.6% to $1.7 billion in the most recent fiscal year from $2.2 billion in the prior year, with gross margin contracting to 20.7% and operating margin at 4.7%. Net income reached $72.6 million despite the revenue decline.

The company recognized $6.7 million in inventory impairment charges across four communities in fiscal 2025, with $3.9 million in the Florida segment and $2.8 million in the Central segment. In 2025, LGI Homes completed a joint venture with Evergreen Residential Capital, LLC, capitalized at $50 million, which supports the expansion of its single-family rental portfolio through the LGI Living financing platform. Wholesale home closings to large institutions for single-family rental properties represented 15.7% of total home closings in 2025, reflecting growth in this channel. Administrative costs run higher than smaller local builders, while capital intensity requires significant upfront land investment. New market entrants face shorter operating histories and relationships. The business depends on subcontractors with no long-term contractual commitments and remains exposed to regional economic downturns, particularly concentrated in five primary markets. Leverage amplifies vulnerability to adverse industry conditions. Wholesale revenue concentration at 15.7% of closings ties performance to institutional buyer demand.

The company is targeting expansion of its Terrata Homes luxury brand to 20 active communities and growth of wholesale business within the 15.7% annual closing target. Community count is shifting to 144 from 151 as management pursues selective land opportunities aligned with land development expertise across multi-price-point segments. ### PZZA

Papa Johns International operates a pizza-centric restaurant business across four segments: domestic company-owned locations, North American franchising, North American commissaries, and international operations. The company generated $2.05 billion in revenue in the filing period, essentially flat year-over-year, with gross margin of 28.9% and operating margin of 4.3%. The business derives most revenue from retail pizza and food sales through 6,083 restaurants across 50 countries, positioning itself on a "BETTER INGREDIENTS. BETTER PIZZA" brand promise supported by quality control centers and digital ordering investments. Primary revenue comes from domestic and North American operations, with the UK and other international markets representing secondary geographies. The company competes against large national pizza chains, regional operators, local independent pizzerias, fast-casual concepts, and food delivery aggregators, alongside grocery stores offering prepared meals.

Papa Johns disclosed material supply chain vulnerabilities and took strategic asset actions in 2025. The company has a sole mozzarella cheese supplier for domestic production and substantially all international cheese, a single source for garlic sauce, and limited supplier options for meat and other key ingredients—creating concentration risk across core product inputs. In 2025, tornadoes damaged quality control centers in Grand Prairie, Texas and Louisville, Kentucky, resulting in $8.6 million in property and equipment and lease asset impairments. The company also completed a $17.1 million asset sale to Colonel's Limited, LLC in 2025, following a $46.7 million asset sale in 2024. These transactions, combined with prior-year UK restaurant closures and an $11.7 million impairment related to 73 UK location exits, signal ongoing portfolio optimization and geographic repositioning.

The business carries structural constraints that distinguish its competitive position. Sole reliance on one mozzarella supplier and limited suppliers for other key ingredients creates operational vulnerability, particularly given supply chain disruptions tied to QC Center damage in 2025. The company acknowledges that competitors possess substantially greater resources and that it faces higher ingredient costs than some rivals, while intense price and promotional competition pressures margins. Distribution through 11 U.S. QC centers and one Canadian center concentrates supply risk; damage or disruption at these facilities directly threatens restaurant supply. The domestic market generates substantial revenue, with ingredients and supplies sourced primarily in the United States. Management also notes vulnerability to consumer preference shifts toward healthier foods and competition for qualified franchisees and drivers.

Forward priorities include an Enterprise Transformation Plan projecting $24–31 million in restructuring charges through 2027, North American supply chain savings of at least $60 million over two years, a new omnichannel platform rollout with $5–10 million in accelerated depreciation, and a multi-year point-of-sale system replacement across U.S. restaurants. The company accelerated domestic refranchising, completing 85 restaurant conversions in Q4 2025. Planned capital expenditure is $70–80 million, centered on $75 million. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided in the filing.

Penguin Solutions, Inc. operates across three distinct business segments serving the high-performance computing and specialty semiconductor markets. The Advanced Computing segment provides HPC and AI infrastructure solutions, fault-tolerant computing platforms, and discontinued Penguin Edge products. The Integrated Memory segment addresses capacity constraints in high-performance systems through DRAM modules, flash storage, and supply chain services. The Optimized LED segment manufactures application-specific LED chips and components under the Cree brand for lighting, displays, and specialty applications. The company maintains primary geographic presence in the United States, China, and Malaysia, with secondary operations across Europe and broader Asia.

Penguin Solutions recorded a $16.1 million goodwill impairment related to the Penguin Edge business in fiscal 2025, following a $19.1 million impairment on the same asset in 2023. The company plans to discontinue the Penguin Edge product portfolio by the end of calendar 2025. These write-downs reflect underperformance in that product line and signal a strategic realignment around core HPC and AI infrastructure. American Eagle Outfitters operates two primary apparel brands: American Eagle, which sells casual, comfortable, and timeless apparel and accessories across all styles, and Aerie, which focuses on intimates, apparel, activewear, and swim collections including the OFFLINE by Aerie activewear brand. The company serves customers across the United States, Canada, and Mexico as primary markets, with secondary presence in Asia, Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East. Revenue grew 4.1% to $5.5 billion in the most recent fiscal year, though gross margin remained compressed at 36.5% and operating margin came in at a slim 4.1%. Product innovation around fabric and jeans styles, combined with inclusive brand positioning emphasizing real representation, form core competitive pillars. These write-downs signal integration challenges and customer retention risk tied to acquisitions.

Chefs' Warehouse operates with gross margin of 24.2% and operating margin of 3.5%, characteristic of the low-margin foodservice distribution industry. The company faces structural headwinds: no single customer represents meaningful revenue concentration (top ten customers account for 6% of sales), but the business remains vulnerable to consumer discretionary spending fluctuations, inflationary and deflationary cost pressures, high labor costs relative to revenues, and supply chain interruptions. Dependence on third-party suppliers without long-term contracts and concentration in certain geographic markets create additional operational risk. The company sources from globally distributed suppliers across North America, Europe, Asia, Australia, South America, and Mediterranean countries, introducing geographic exposure.

Management has committed to $45–55 million in capital expenditures, centered on distribution center construction in Las Vegas, Oman, Denver, Portland, San Francisco, Philadelphia, and Miami. The company is implementing a supply chain planning system, optimizing its e-commerce platform with AI and search capabilities, deploying warehouse wearable inventory scanning devices, and extended its asset-based loan facility through August 2030. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided.

### KWR
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/81362/000162828026010694/kwr-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: none._

Quaker Chemical Corp is a global supplier of specialty industrial process fluids and chemical management services. The company operates across three geographic segments—Americas, EMEA, and Asia/Pacific—with primary exposure to the United States, Europe, and Asia/Pacific region, supplemented by operations in Brazil, Mexico, and China. Its product portfolio spans metal removal fluids, rolling lubricants, hydraulic fluids, surface solutions, cleaning fluids, corrosion inhibitors, metal drawing and forming fluids, die cast mold releases, heat treatment and quenchants, and specialty greases, among others. Quaker positions itself as a global leader in industrial process fluids with leading positions in automotive and industrial process fluids markets and in process fluids for sheet steel and aluminum production. The company supports this positioning through an extensive network of 30 laboratory facilities worldwide and 10 principal laboratories for advanced research, direct sales via its own employees, proprietary FluidcareTM chemical management services, and proprietary formulas and applications know-how. Revenue grew 2.7% to $1.89 billion in fiscal 2025, though profitability deteriorated significantly: gross margin remained flat at 36%, but operating margin compressed to 2.8%, and the company reported a net loss of $2.5 million.

A substantial goodwill impairment charge of $88.8 million in the EMEA segment during 2025 reflects material headwinds. The company attributed this impairment to soft end market conditions and increased cost of capital driven by tariff uncertainty. This impairment underscores deteriorating regional performance and signals management's reassessment of previously acquired assets' sustainable value in the current macroeconomic environment.

Customer concentration remains modest, with the five largest customers accounting for approximately 11% of consolidated net sales in 2025 and the largest single customer representing approximately 3%. However, the company faces structural vulnerabilities inherent to its business model. Demand is derived from customers' product demand and subject to business cycles, and the company has disclosed an inability to adjust costs contemporaneously with sales changes. Raw material price volatility presents exposure, and management has flagged difficulty passing through raw material cost increases to customers. The company also identified a limited patent portfolio with earliest expiry in 2026, placing heavy reliance on proprietary formulas rather than patent protection. Supply chain dependencies exist in Japan and China. Competitive positioning against specialty and larger chemical companies, along with risk of customer consolidation and loss of market share, represent additional structural concerns.

During 2025, Quaker completed three acquisitions—Dipsol Chemicals Co., Ltd., Natech, Ltd., and Chemical Solutions & Innovations (Pty) Ltd.—to expand advanced solutions and strengthen surface treatment capabilities in Europe. Earlier, in 2024, the company acquired Sutai Group and I.K.V. Tribologie IKVT. The company is executing a global cost and optimization program targeting approximately $40 million in annualized savings by the end of 2026, supported by restructuring that has reduced headcount and closed facilities. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided for the forward period.

ScanSource distributes technology hardware, software, and services through two operating segments. The Specialty Technology Solutions segment operates in the United States, Canada, and Brazil, offering a broad range of products including mobility and barcode solutions, point-of-sale systems, payment terminals, physical security, networking, and connectivity through a wholesale and resale model. The Intelisys & Advisory segment operates in the United States as a technology services distributor using an agency model, focusing on cloud, connectivity, and next-generation technologies with recurring revenue from SaaS and subscription services. The company positions itself on deep technical specialization, industry-leading custom configuration capabilities, comprehensive solutions engineering, and the ability to operate through multiple sales models with variable cost structures and strong supplier relationships.

Revenue declined 6.7% to $3.04 billion in fiscal 2025 from $3.26 billion in the prior year. Gross margin stood at 13.4%, reflecting the compressed pricing environment the company discloses as a structural disadvantage. Operating margin was 2.8%, with net income of $71.5 million. The company completed two strategic acquisitions in 2024: the purchase of Secure Path Networks, LLC (Resourcive) to expand IT sourcing solutions and the acquisition of Advantix Solutions Group, Inc. to strengthen wireless enablement offerings. The company also executed a cost reduction and restructuring program that is expected to deliver $20.5 million in annual savings. Additionally, ScanSource extended the maturity of its multi-currency revolving credit facility to September 2027 and maintains a share repurchase program with $217.1 million available.

ScanSource faces structural constraints typical of its distribution model. Cisco and Zebra products each constitute more than 10% of net sales, creating material supply concentration risk. No single channel partner represents more than 10% of sales, indicating reasonable customer diversification. The company competes against broad-line distributors (Ingram Micro, TD Synnex, ADI, Wesco), specialized competitors (BlueStar, Avant, Telarus), and direct suppliers. The stated disadvantages reveal the core tension in the business: narrow operating margins driven by price competition, inventory obsolescence risk, dependence on third-party shippers, and vulnerability to supplier consolidation. Centralized operations present single points of failure risk.

Capital allocation remains moderate, with planned capex of $12.5 million (within a $10–15 million range). The company provided no forward revenue or earnings guidance.

### PRVA
